wish to direct the attention of the Prime Minister to a despatch appearing in the press this morning with reference to a debate in the English House of Lords with regard to Canada's attitude toward the signing of the optional clause. I made a
statement in the house in this connection some time ago, and since the morning papers have a reference to what was then said it might be well for me to read my remarks on that occasion. On February 19 I made a short statement which is all I have said in this connection and which covers the position of the Canadian government with respect to the optional clause. That statement is found at page 248 of Hansard and was made in answer to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) as follows:
My hon. friend will recall that during the last imperial conference a desire was expressed on the part of the governments assembled there that no one part of the British Empire should formally accept the optional clause without giving to the other parts of the empire an opportunity of discussing that particular subject. We have advised the other parts of the empire that in our opinion Canada should sign the optional clause, and we are at present receiving communications from other parts of the empire in reference thereto. We are carrying out our undertaking at the conference not to sign formally until there has been an opportunity for discussion, but we have made known that it is our desire to sign the optional clause.
I noticed that in the press report there seemed to be an impression that I had expressed some view as to what other parts of the empire were to do with respect to the optional clause. I expressed no such view either at that time or at any other time; I spoke in reference to Canada only. So far as we are concerned our correspondence could be brought down at any time, with the consent of the governments with which we have been corresponding.

Mr. Chairman, I do not think that I would be doing my duty if I allowed this vote to pass without commenting on many of the statements which were made yesterday by the Postmaster General (Mr. Veniot) in defence of his department. It would -take at least two hours to make out the full case and spread it on Hansard. The Postmaster General said that he would deal with a certain number of postmasterships as they came under the Civil Service Aict. He dealt with Haiwkedbury, Alexandria, New Glasgow, Brigden, St. Boniface, Brussels, East St. John, Oliver, Norton, and one or two others. If the Postmaster General made similar misrepresentations with reference to all the other post offices as he did concerning Norton then his argument falls very flat and there is not one word of truth in the utterances of the hon. gentleman with regard to Norton.
Order.

This is what the Postmaster General stated yesterday.
I know that I am taking up a good deaf of the time of the house, but I think it is worth While. The next case is that of Norton in the province of New Brunswick. This position was declared vacant before my time and after an investigation as to political partisanship against the postmaster named Price. When I entered office I found that a returned soldier by the name of Ward had received a certificate from the Civil Service Commission. Considerable turmoil had been created before I took charge. I intended to start with a clean sheet and I declared

that this vacancy still existed and asked for new advertisements. Some time elapsed before this was done, because the case at Norton was not called to my attention until some time in 1927.
The Postmaster General as a responsible member of the cabinet and the present administration says that this matter was not called to his attention until 1928, but before I am through I intend to prove to the satisfaction of any reasonable person in this country that the Postmaster General did know-all about the Norton .case as far back as 1924 -when he was the premier of the province of New Brunswick. The Postmaster General's statement continues:
In the meantime Mr. Price, who was a very old man

I might state that he is not as old as the Postmaster General.
-was left in charge of the office although he had been found guilty of political partizanship. I understand that Mr. Ward was the victim of a very serious automobile accident.
I interjected at this point and said:
It was another returned soldier by the name of Harmer.
Then the Postmaster General continued:
I am coming to that case. I declared the office vacant and called for new advertisements.
I was ref erring to Mr. Price.
No, you referred to Mr. Ward and I corrected you. Mr. Harmer was iu an automobile accident as well.
I did not know that.

Oh yes, you knew Mr. Harmer. The statement continues:
The Civil Service Commission advised me that if I wanted to do that I would have to dispose of the certificate already issued in favour of Ward. I did so, and the vacancy was advertised and I believe Ward is an applicant as well as Harmer. At the present time a civilian is temporarily in charge of the office with the distinct understanding that it is only temporary and that returned soldiers with qualifications are to have preference. That is the Norton case as it now stands and no decision has been reached as yet in that case.
I intend to deal with the case from March, 1924. Order in Council, P.C. 326, dated March 7, 1924, was passed for the dismissal of Allan Price. A letter was written by Hon. Charles Murphy, the then Postmaster General, to Doctor McAllister, the defeated Liberal candidate in 1921, informing him that Mr. Price had been, dismissed by order in council and that he had better send in an applicant for the position. Dr. McAllister replied' to the

Supply-Post Office
then. Postmaster General stating that as this was a very important office he wanted to see a good man appointed. This occurred on March 11.
A letter dated March 17, 1924, was written by Dr. McAllister to Hon. Charles Murphy recommending William A. Reynolds, which stated that reasons would be given later on. This Norton file which appears to be stripped of a good deal of the correspondence does not contain any letter setting forth the further reasons why Mr. Reynolds should be appointed. In his letter of March 7 to Dr. McAllister, Mr. Murphy referred to the faot that Mr. Reynolds had been recommended by Hon. P. J. Yeniot, premier of the province of New Brunswick. The Postmaster General now comes forward and states that he knew nothing about this case until he assumed office.
On March 21 a letter was written by Mr. Coolican to the district superintendent at St. John with reference to advertising the position. I have all the papers under my hand, but as I said before, it would be impossible to read all the correspondence.
On May 29 notice of the advertisement was posted, signed by W. Foran, Secretary of the Civil Service Commission.
On May 28 there is a letter from W. H. Heine, enclosing a petition signed by ninety-two residents of Norton in favour of the retention of Mr. Price.
On April 15, 1924, there is a letter from Mr. L J. Gaboury, Deputy Postmaster General, to the district superintendent at St. John re Fred E. Sharp, an applicant for the position. I may say that Mr. Fred E. Sharp was the defeated Liberal candidate in the 1917 federal election, and he was also on a previous occasion a defeated candidate for the New Brunswick legislature. This letter called the attention of the district superintendent to the fact that Mr. Sharp was an applicant and asked him to put Mr. Sharp's name on the list of applicants for the postmastership at Norton.
On April 15 there is a telegram from Doctor McAllister to the Hon. Charles Murphy, then Postmaster General, asking him to carry out his recommendation regarding Mr. Reynolds, but giving no further information as to his qualifications or why the position should be given to him over the heads of a large number of returned soldiers.
On April 17 there is another letter from Mr. L. J. Gaboury, Deputy Postmaster General, to Doctor McAllister, pointing out that the Norton post office was under the Civil Service Commission.
On May 8, 1924, there is a report from the district superintendent to the Postmaster General, stating that ten applications had been received for the Norton post office. I wish to pause at this point for a moment or two in order to give the ratings of the different applicants for that office. The report from the district superintendent is dated St. John, New Brunswick, May 8, 1924, and it contains nine pages. I will just give a list of the applicants:
George Ward, a returned solder.
Ivan William Reid, a returned soldier.
Fred E. Sharp.
Miss Lucy Jane Campbell.
William A. Reynolds.
Ernest Nelson Myers.
William E. Harmer, a returned soldier.
This man enlisted in the 104 battalion. After he had enlisted he was taken with appendicitis. He was operated on and could not go to the front, but later on he went to work in a munitions plant and did everything he could to help win the war.
Miss Mary E. Saunders, Bloomfield Station.
Preston Douglas Price, a returned soldier formerly of Norton, but now of Concord, New Hampshire.
Charles Thomas Homer, Southfield, N.B.
That is five miles from Norton. It would take up too much time to read the whole report and I do not wish to dwell on the matter any longer than necessary. I will now give the report of the district superintendent in regard to George Ward, as follows:
Educational qualification:	Good common
school education in England.
Accommodation offered: Suitable.
Location offered: Present site.
Residential qualifications: Has been living in the vicinity of Norton since April, 1921.
Experience: A little post office experience and has had experience in meeting the public.
Character and integrity: Good.
Time willing to give to post office: Full time.
AVhether returned soldier: Yes.
Whether disability case: No,-but is in receipt of a small pension.
That was the report on. Mr. Ward, No. 1 on the whole list. There were practically as good reports on Ivan William Reid, another returned soldier; William Elias Harmer, a returned soldier; Preston Douglas Price, another returned soldier who saw service in France; and Charles Thomas Homer, another returned soldier who saw service at the front, and who, by the way, was a school teacher before he went to the war.
I wish to give a further report regarding George Ward, the man who received the certificate from the Civil Service Commission:
Mr. George Ward; twenty-eight years of age; unmarried; is a returned soldier who enlisted in 1915; went overseas in 1916 and saw service at Vimy Ridge, Hill 70 and Passchendaele;

Supply-Post Office

was wounded in November, 1917, and lost two fingers of his left hand; was discharged January, 1919, and is in receipt of a small pension per month. After his return from the war he took a course through the vocational department of the Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment, and has been employed as a telegraph operator on and off at intervals since March 6, 1920. For the past three months has been a clerk in the store of W. A. Saunders, at Bloomfield station in the parish of Norton six miles distant from Norton. He has had a little post office experience, having assisted the postmaster at Bloomfield station during the period the office was in Mr. Saunders' store (about one year). He is a man of good appearance, and comes well recommended by the members of the Empire Soldiers Club at Norton; by the secretary-treasurer of the G.W.V.A., and by King and McDonald, wholesale grocers of St. John; by the chief train dispatcher of the Canadian National Railways, Moncton, N.B., and by the Anglican Bishop of Fredericton, as per letters herewith enclosed.
There are no recommendations on the file. The file has been stripped of all those.
After his return from the war Mr. Ward met with an accident in a saw-mill which crippled his right hand slightly but his war and other injuries would not in any way interfere with his carrying on post office work. If appointed, Mr. Ward would provide a suitable location for the post office.
I do not intend to take up any more time. As I stated, this report of the district superintendent is nine pages long. I wish to lay this case before the committee in order that it may be judged on its merits.
On May 14, 1924, there is a letter and a petition from William E. Harmer, returned soldier, who had enlisted in the 104th battalion. This was sent to the Hon. Charles Stewart, at that time Acting Postmaster General.
On May 20 there is a letter from the Deputy Postmaster General to Doctor McAllister informing him again-there is no reference on the file to any letter from the doctor-that returned soldiers would have the preference under the Civil Service Act, as it is the law of the country. The Deputy Postmaster General who wrote that letter is the same deputy who is in charge to-day.
Next is a letter, dated May 27th, from William E. Harmer to the Hon. Charles Murphy, the then Postmaster General, informing him of Ward's record and of his joining the 104th battalion, and so on. It is a very long letter.
Then appears the certificate of the Civil Sendee Commission, dated July 30, 1924, of the apointment of George Ward as postmaster at Norton. I might point out that there were no strings attached to this certificate, as was the case, I understand, with some others.

This was a straight certificate appointing Mr. George Ward, postmaster at Norton.
About a week later, Mr. E. J. Undenvood, chief superintendent of post office service, writes to Mr. W. A. Reynolds, one of the applicants, informing him of the appointment of Mr. George Ward as postmaster at Norton.
Then on August 8, 1924, Doctor McAllister writes to the Hon, A. B. Copp, Secretary of State, as follows:
I am writing you again re Norton P.O. affair Little did I expect the Civil Service would choose Geo. Ward, not only for his being an emigrant to this country but for his incapabilities. It is true that he was overseas but he has been fully compensated since his return. The federal government gave him a course in telegraphy and the local government has compensated him to the extent of five hundred dollars, and I have learned to-day that his employer who runs a general store and had him as a cleTk. discharged him for cause. His employer was F. Saunders. Bloomfield, lumber man and merchant, I think this matter should be looked into. Please call the attention of this to the Postmaster General and by so doing you will greatly oblige.
Mr. McAllister was the defeated Liberal candidate in 1921, again in 1925, and again in 1926, and this is the kind of stuff that the local Liberal organization in the constituency of Royal kept putting up to the Postmaster General.
There is a lot of correspondence following the charge that Ward was a defaulter, and finally the matter came into the court at St. John, and after being considered by the grand jury it was thrown out. The correspondence which was furnished to the Civil Service Commission is here, and it shows that there was absolutely nothing in the charge and that it could not be proven.
On August 12, 1924, Hon. Charles Murphy writes to Mr. Copp acknowledging receipt of this letter from Doctor McAllister, saying that Ward had been appointed according to the law and under the Civil Service Commission. I want to emphasize, Mr. Chairman, that this was on August 12, 1924. For nearly two years from that time, until November 17, 1926, there was not much activity in this matter. During all this time the old postmaster was in charge, the man who had been dismissed by order in council. The former Postmaster General, the Hon. Charles Murphy, did not make any move to override the Civil Service Commission, but just as soon as the present Postmaster General assumed office on August 17, 1926, action took place. I will read this letter in full. It is written by the present Postmaster General

Supply-Post Office
to the chairman of the Civil Service Commission, and is dated Ottawa, November 17, 1926:
Chairman,
Civil Service Commission,
Ottawa, Ont.
Gentlemen:
I understand that the vacancy for the Norton post office, Queens county, N.B.-
By the way, it is Kings, not Queens county; it is in the constituency of Royal:
[DOT]-lias been standing for a considerable time. It appears that serious objections have been raised to the appointment of one Ward, who, I understand, ranks first in the qualification examination for that position, followed by one Reynolds.
I further understand that your board issued a certificate of appointment in favour of Mr. Ward, but that he was not installed in office, and the former postmaster who was found guilty of political partisanship still remaining in charge of the office.
The hon. Postmaster General knew that this man was in office all the time, and preferred to keep Mr. Price there rather than appoint Mr. Ward, a returned soldier, to the office, as recommended by the Civil Service Commission. The letter continues:
With the knowledge that he had obtained this appointment, Mr. Ward, in the last election took a very active part. My information is that he was even obnoxious in his conduct to those who did not agree with him in politics. In view of this, I feel that Mr. Ward should not now be allowed to take advantage of the certificate that has been issued in his favour.
I would ask that your board give this matter very serious consideration.
The chairman of the Civil Service Commission, Doctor Roche, replied as follows, under date of November 20, 1926:
Dear Mr. Veniot:
I desire to acknowledge yours of the 17th, in which you refer to the fact that Mr. Ward ffor whose appointment as postmaster at Norton. Queens county, N.B. a certificate was issued by the commission some two years ago) took an active part in the recent general election, and expressing your view that Mr. Ward should not now be allowed to take advantage of the certificate issued in his favour.
Unfortunately, however, once a certificate of appointment has been issued by the commission the matter passes beyond the jurisdiction of this body, but I have placed your letter before the full board of the commission, and as the commission is awaiting the decision of the Department of Justice on a point in connection with another case that has a bearing on this case, you will be further advised after the commission has received the opinion of the Department of Justice on the point referred to.
Following the receipt of that letter, the Postmaster General did not lose very much time, for on November 24 he writes from his
78594-138}
office at Ottawa to the Hon. W. J. Roche, chairman of the Civil Service Commission, as follows:
My dear Sir:
I am in receipt of yours of the 20th in reply to mine of the 17th in which I called your attention to the fact that Mr. Ward (for whose appointment as postmaster at Norton. Queens County, N.B., a certificate was issued by the commission some two years ago) had taken an active part in the last federal election and for that reason I did not think that he should finally receive the appointment of postmaster at Norton. I note what, you say about a certificate being once issued that the matter passes beyond the jurisdiction of your commission, but that you have placed my letter before the full board of the commission, and as the commission is awaiting the decision from the Department of Justice on a point in connection with another case that has a bearing on this case, I will be further advised in the matter after you receive the opinion of the Justice department.
A few days after that the chairman of the Civil Service Commission, Doctor Roche, wrote the following letter:
December 2, 1926.
Dear Mr. Veniot,
In further reference to the postmastership at Norton, Queens County, N.B., in mine of the-20th ultimo I pointed out that the commission's jurisdiction in regard to this appointment ceased after issuing the certificate in favour of Mr. Ward. But owing to another case having: been referred to the Department of Justice for-decision which might have a bearing upon this case I promised to let you know when such opinion was received.
The opinion referred to was in connection with the Hawkesbury postmastership, as to whether a department could legally reject a candidate for whom a certificate had been issued by the commission when more than one year had elapsed since the issue of such certificate.
The opinion just received from the Department of Justice is to the effect that section 13 may be invoked in rejecting a candidate after twelve months had elapsed from the date of certificate unless the person sought to be rejected has served in the position for a probationary period for six or tw-elve months, as the case may be. In the Hawkesbury case, however, 1 understand that your point is that the candidate for whom the commission issued its certificate of appointment is not sufficiently qualified bilingually, notwithstanding both the departmental officers and the commission decided otherwise, and if you feel justified in rejecting this candidate under section 13, apparently you can legally do so according to the decision of the Department of Justice. But in the case of the Norton postmastership you object to Mr. Ward being allowed to take advantage of the certificate issued in his favor by the reason of his activities in connection with the recent Dominion elections. I do not think this would be sufficient ground for the department to refuse to instal Mr. Ward in office, as he is not civil servant until he has been placed in a position to discharge the duties of same. Otherwise if he did not have the office tranferred to him for the next ten or fifteen years he might have his
Supply-Post Office

hands tied politically notwithstanding he was earning his livelihood entirely outside the service, and this does not seem at all reasonable.
It would appear to me therefore that if it is your intention to reject Mr. Ward under section 13 some more substantial reason should be assigned than the one to which you refer. I think if you will discuss this point with the Deputy Minister of Justice he will agree with me.
You see by this correspondence between the Postmaster General and the Civil Service Commission that there was a desperate effort made to get rid of Mr. Ward, who had been appointed postmaster at Norton. On August 28, 1928, after an interval of almost two years from the date of the letter I have just read, there was a lot of correspondence between the department and the Postmaster General. I wish to refer to a letter of August 28, 1928, written by the Hon. P. J. Veniot, Postmaster General, to Mr. Gaboury:
Dismiss Allan Price and appoint William A. Reynolds acting postmaster at Norton.
This was done in face of the letter from the Civil Service Commission setting out the law in regard to this case.
On August 31 there is a letter from E. J. Underwood to the district superintendent at St. John, instructing him to put into the office Mr. W. A. Reynolds as acting postmaster.
On September 7, 1928, I find a letter from H. W. Woods to the superintendent of postal service saying that Mr. Reynolds had been installed on September 15.
On September 14 there is a letter from Mr. B. E. Thomas, Service Bureau of the Canadian Legion of British Empire Service League, to the Hon. Mr. Veniot, asking him why Mr. Ward had not been called upon to fill the post office at Norton. I desire to read the letter in reply from the Postmaster General. It is dated September 19, 1928:
Dear Sir,-
I am in receipt of yours of the 14th instant m connection with the postmastership at Norton, N.B., and in reply beg to give you the following information:
It appears that in 1924, two years before I assumed the position of Postmaster General, an investigation was held into the conduct of the postmaster at Norton, N.B., and the charges made against him were investigated and proven. The office was declared vacant, but he was allowed to remain in temporary charge until the Civil Service Commission had made a permanent appointment. George Ward, a returned soldier, was one of the applicants, and he received the certificate of the Civil Service Commission for the permanent appointment. This certificate, it appears, was never accepted by the Postmaster General. The matter was left in abeyance with the old postmaster still acting when I took charge of this department. 
Now, I desire hon. members to listen to this. The letter continues:
I knew nothing about this matter. About a year ago my attention was called to the situation at Norton, and after making inquiries touching the details I decided that in view of the length of time that had expired between the date of advertising the vacancy in 1924, and the time that the matter had been drawn to my attention, and in view of the fact that I learned that Ward had left Norton and was engaged in a position at St. John, and that there were other returned soldiers who had applied and who were still residing in Norton, it would be better under all the circumstances to have the vacancy advertised anew. In the meantime, so as to give no undue advantage to one returned soldier as against another, I issued instructions to have this vacancy advertised and to appoint a Mr. Reynolds in temporary charge. I had to appoint a person in temporary charge because conditions were such as Norton that it was impossible to put up any longer with the old gentleman in charge.
You will notice that in this letter the Postmaster General states that the matter has only just been drawn to his attention, whereas two yeans previously he had taken the matter up himself with the Civil Service Commission,
As Postmaster General?

Yes, as Postmaster General,
in 1926. And this letter is 1928. In November and December, 1926, he had taken the matter up, and here he says he knew nothing about it. Perhaps I have taken up more time on this matter than I should otherwise have done, but it is one of the most important questions that can be directed to the attention of the house. On October 4,	1928, there was
addressed, from J. G. Herwig, of the British Empire Service League, a letter to the Hon. Mr. Veniot, calling his attention again to the matter of Mr. Ward's not receiving the appointment. And then we have another letter, October 5, 1928, from L. D. Theriault, secretary, to Mr. Herwig.

I have a few words to say on this matter. I heard- the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Clark) say this afternoon that he wished to have the will of parliament expressed; I think it is rather the wish of the opposition that he wants to see fulfilled.
I do not understand how it can be said that persons who have been appointed temporarily by the Postmaster General, pending permanent appointment by the Civil Service Commission, should not be paid. In my opinion the most important thing is to have the office running continuously. Suppose a postmaster dies or is unable to fulfil his duties; surely it is the duty of the Postmaster General to prevent what I may call a break in the service rendered by that particular post office; and to this end he must appoint someone temporarily to carry out the duties of the office pending appointment by the Civil Service Commission, and the person in charge shall be paid for performing such service.
We have heard a lot this afternoon about the Civil Service Act. I have here the French text of the act, chapter 22 of the revised statutes of 1927; and there is another act also which is of utmost importance in this connection, and which has been overlooked by all hon. gentlemen on the other side ever since they began discussing the estimates of the Post Office Department. I refer to the Post Office Act. If I understood what my hon. friend from Vancouver-Burrard said this afternoon, the minister has nothing to do in his department. For example, according to the hon. gentleman, in the event of a vacancy occurring it should be filled temporarily by a district superintendent, who would report to the Postmaster General advising him accordingly, and if that temporary appointment were not satisfactory, then -the Postmaster General would advise his officer of his dissatisfaction and would cancel the appointment and make another. This, it seems to me, is the. very reverse of what should be done. Under the statute the power is not
Supply-Post Office

given primarily to the subordinate, the employee, the officer of the department; it is vested in the minister who is at the head of all authority in the department. This is how I understand the law in this matter and 1 think it is but fair; it is common sense; otherwise we should have a state of insubordination.
There is another point to be considered: When there are two acts dealing with the same subject we must take those acts jointly in order to understand the intent of parliament. This is a principle which is understood not only by lawyers but even by ordinary business men in the country. Now here is a point of considerable importance in relation to this question. According to sections 19, 20 and 21 of chapter 22, the Civil Service Act, who is supposed to instruct the Civil Service Commission as to whom they are to appoint in case a vacancy occurs? Let us take the case of a postmaster in some village or town: he dies; suppose it is deemed urgent to appoint a successor immediately so that there may be no break in the continuity of the service. The question is, who will tell the Civil Service Commission what man is to replace temporarily the late postmaster?
Taschereau.
St. Peter of Cape Breton. My hon. friend usually has very much brains in his hand.

Taschereau.
I see my hon. friend wants to change his leader.

Yesterday the Postmaster
General made a statement in regard to the returning officers. I did not intend to mention this, but it does not do to let the hon. gentleman away with all these wild statements. I want to direct the attention of the committee to the incidents connected with the appointment of the postmaster at Oliver, British Columbia, to which passing allusion was made by the Postmaster General yesterday afternoon. The late postmaster at that place desired to resign -last fall, on being appointed customs officer at the neighbouring port of Osoyoos. The post office inspector at Vancouver interviewed these three applicants and reported on them to the Postmaster General. He placed them in a certain order of merit. The first name that appears we can set aside,
fMr. Jones.]
because, as the inspector points out, his military discharge papers were not in order. Is the hon. member reading from the certificate that was found on the file?
Yes.

The certificate found on
the file is not the same class of certificate that is sent to the appointee. All the certificates sent to the appointees have that ruling printed on them and' do not go to the Department.

So that the file which
has been brought down is not an actual copy of the original papers?
What you are reading is only notice to the department of his appointment, not a notice to the appointee. The latter is different.

But surely these papers
that are brought down for the use of the house purport to be exact copies of the original papers.
I do not wish to interrupt the hon. gentleman, but there is an error there.
Does my hon. friend say there is an error here?

No, no. The hon. gentleman is reading from a certificate which he says went to the appointee. That certificate never went to the appointee. The Civil Service Commission sends to the appointee a certificate

which is somewhat different from the one which it sends to us notifying us that an appointment has been made. On the certificate sent by the Civil Service Commission to the appointee is printed the ruling of the Justice department, but it is not on the one sent to us.
Mr. Chairman, in this file which was brought down with reference to the Oliver matter, this certificate appears which purports to be a copy of whait was sent to Anderson.
It does not. The hon. gentleman is wrong. He is making an unfair statement; he is not stating the case right.
Then I would ask the Postmaster General to state it. Where is the mistake?

There are two forms of certificate. The hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Stewart) has a copy of the certificate which is sent to the appointee, I believe, judging by the colour; it is a purple certificate. I think that is the one that is sent to the appointee.
This is a notice of appointment to the postmaster. It is not a certificate.
It contains the ruling of the Justice department.
It does not contain it all, but only part of it as has been pointed out several times.
It contains what the commission thought was sufficient to guide the appointee.
I do not know about that.
What is the use of making statements that are not according to the facts?

I received these papers which set out what has happened with regard to this matter, and I certainly took it that this paper, which is called a certificate of appointment, was a copy of what was sent to the man.
It is not.

If the Postmaster General says that that is not the case, we will drop that point and pass on, but it seems a most extraordinary thing to hand us a file which purports to be the file connected with the case, but which does not contain the papers which were used in this matter.
You have everything from the department there.

Anderson, at all events, receives notice of his selection: I suppose the Postmaster General will agree to that. It is intimated to him that he has been selected. There is a suggestion at least that he will be appointed on probation, and he is told that he will receive instructions as to the date upon which he shall begin his work. I maintain that when a man receives a statement to that effect, bis reaction to it is that he has been successful in the examination held by the Civil Service Commission1, that he will be appointed on probation and will have to start work on a certain day. That at any rate is what entered Anderson's head. He disposed of his stock, altered his premises, bought certain fixtures, and retained the services of an assistant.
Just a month later, early in February, there is a letter from the Postmaster General .to his deputy which refers to the fact that the Postmaster General is in receipt of certain-information which shows that Anderson has; become the agent or local manager of a telephone company in that place. There is nothing on this file to show what is the-source of the Postmaster General's information. It is scarcely likely that the details of the poatmastership in a little place ike Giver, three thousand miles from here, would have been told by word of mouth to the Postmaster General, and I cannot help thinking that some communication must have been received by the Postmaster General which does not appear on this file. The deputy head accordingly writes to the superintendent of the postal service at Vancouver, and suggests that some guarded inquiries should be made to ascertain when Anderson took charge of the telephone company. Eventually the Postmaster General receives that information in the form of a communication signed by Mr. Murray of the superintendent's department in Vancouver, confirming -the fact that Mr. Anderson has been made agent for the local telephone company, and that he started operations on the 1st of February. I would draw the attention of the committee to the fact that ever since Oliver has had a post office the holder of that postmastership has also been agent of the local -telephone company. To urge that connection as a good reason for rejecting the selection of the Civil Service Commission is not a reason -but a flimsy excuse. It takes six days for a letter to pass betwen Oliver and Ottawa, and a little more than a week after the Postmaster General communicated with his deputy asking him to ascertain details with regard to this telephone position, two letters are written from Oliver to the Postmaster General, which
Supply-Post Office

I shall put on record as they are very short. The first one is dated Oliver, February 18, and reads:
The Hon. the Postmaster General,
Ottawa, Ontario.
Honourable Sir:
In behalf of myself and others doing business at Oliver I take the liberty of respectfully requesting you that the post office be not put in with the telephone service, and also desiring that you would favourably consider the application for the postmastership sent in by Mr. H. A. Ede as we believe he is a suitable and competent person for the position.
Sincerely yours,
(Signed) A. L. Rhynd.
Then follows a letter dated at Oliver, dated February 19, 1929, to the hon. Postmaster General:
Dear Sir,

It has always been a bone of contention here, the post office and telephone office in together, the service has been very poor. They are unable to give good service in either line. We understand Mr. Anderson, who has the telephone office, has an application for the post office as well, to which 90 per cent of the pepole here object, I am sure. There is another qualified applicant who we are sure would give good service, a Mr. Ede, who is qualified in every respect. I am sure this will voice the sentiment of a very large majority of the people of this district.
Thanking you for any consideration of this letter, I am,
Yours very truly,
William Foster,
Oliver Confectionery and Tonsorial.
There is no evidence whatever, Mr. Chairman, that the Postmaster General made any attempt to get confirmation of these statements. It would appear therefore that all that is necessary, when the desire for the rejection of a Civil Service Commission appointee is in the mind of the Postmaster General is that he should receive a letter, or perhaps his limit is two, containing any statement the author cares to make, and then the Postmaster General will accept those statements as a reason for the action he takes. Had he taken the trouble to get confirmation of the statements to which I have referred, I think these facts would have been revealed to him: that William Foster is the man who sold a vacant lot next his barber shop to Mr. Ede, and that the writer of the other letter has leased his ten-foot frontage to Mr. Ede, to be used for the new post office. Both of them, one would consider, rather biased witnesses, and I think further inquiry in the locality would have proved to him that these two men, Foster , and Rhynd, were about the only two supporters in the whole district that Mr. Ede had.

I suggest that the Postmaster General has set at naught the appointment of Anderson, who was acceptable in the eyes of the minister's own superintendent, and who has appointed by the Civil Service Commission. I do not understand why the Postmaster General should adopt this course. I do not understand why the government should set at naught the provisions of the Civil Service Act. I will say this much for the government, speaking as I do of four or five years' representation of that piece of southern British Columbia: I should be inclined to state that in the matter of these appointments the various departments of this government have been reasonnably fair, have reasonably left partisanship out of their appointments until now, and it has remained for the Postmaster General to spray this poison into that district of British Columbia. I do not know what effect the Postmaster General desires to obtain, but I think I know what the effect of his action will be. He has certainly made it far more difficult for the next Liberal candidate in the riding of Yale to get elected. He has certainly made it more difficult in the whole of souther British Columbia to instil into the minds of the people that this government is desirous of upholding the Civil Service Act. And I can assure him that the people of British Columbia desire to uphold it; they do not wish to see it flouted. And he has set this government at variance with the Canadian Legion. I would draw the attention of the committee to the two closing paragraphs of a letter adressed to the Postmaster General by J. C. G. Herwig, Service Bureau, Canadian Legion of the British Empire Service League. The letter is dated April 5, 1929. These are the paragraphs to which I refer:
May we ask whether favourable consideration can be given to a claim toy Mr. Anderson for reimbursement of expenses? We are sure that anyone applying for a position in the federal service should not suffer loss on that account, particularly after obtaining success in an open competition.
The views of the Canadian Legion in regard to the spirit in which rejections are carried out has already been made known to you. We regret that another case should have arisen where an ex-service man, after considerable delay, has^ been rejected on the grounds of "unsuitability" without a trial in the position.
That, I think, fairly reflects the opinion of the returned men in Canada, and also I think of the great body of civil servants from the Atlantic to the Pacific; they feel rather more nervous than they did as to the retention of their positions because of the conduct of the Postmaster General.

Re fiscal year 1921-22

Had it not been for this extra outlay the operations of the department for the year would have shown a very material surplus.
Those rates were fixed by the railway commission as the result of an application by the railways for increased rates at so much per foot for the use of mail cars.

-the estimated savings on this account being at the rate of $400,000 per annum.

The discontinuance of the use of postage stamps in the payment of war tax on cheques, etc., effective from 1st October, 1923, resulted in a decrease in revenue while the expenditure on account of salaries of postal employees and supplies generally accounted for the reduction in surplus of approximately $600,000.
For the years 1916 to 1924 the figures giving the revenue of the department, included postage stamps used in payment of war tax. Had it not been for this source of income the operations of the department during _ those years would have shown a decided deficit each year.

Increases in certain other items are practically offset by decreases in the remaining items. The decrease would have been much greater had it not been for increased returns from other classes of mail matter and from other postal facilities. On the other hand expenditure was $500,000 higher than the preceding year, consisting largely of statutory increases and additional positions totalling nearly $400,000, also of added expense for mail service and equipment. These items account for the spread of approximately $2,150,000 between the surplus of the preceding year and the deficit in 1926-27.

The introduction of two cent postage would have affected the remuneration of postmasters who are paid by a percentage on revenue had it not been for the decision of the government that the salaries of these officers should hot be reduced. That is to say, an order in council was passed providing that the salaries should remain the same after as before the reduction from three to two cents.

We were only half through the explanation I was asking from the Postmaster General with regard to the financial end of his department. The net revenue for the year amounted to $30,529,154.76 and the expenditure to $32,379,195 65. This is an increase in the net revenue of $1,150,458.21, instead of the expected decrease due to two cent postage having been m operation for twelve months as compared witn nine months of the previous year; and it indicates a marked increase in the volume of all classes of mail matter.
So I take it that after all there was no loss in net revenue through the reduction in the postage rate. As I have said, the statement shows an increase in revenue so I submit that the decrease in postage rate cannot account for the deficit; the larger volume of business seems to have made up for the reduction in rates. Now I would like to ask the Postmaster General in what year the reduction became effective.
I think it was October 1, 1926.

Then we find tha* in 1927 there was a loss in revenue of only $2,000,000 instead of the $6,000,000 stated by the Postmaster General.

I did not say there was a loss of revenue of $6,000,000; I said if there had been no increase in the volume of business, by one fell stroke of the pen the reduction would have been $6,000,000, but there was a large increase in the volume of business.
So it is quite clear there was no loss of $6,000,000 in revenue.

I would like to refer to the
matter of salaries paid in the postal department. Could the Postmaster General give the committee the amount of increase he recommended to the Civil Service Commission should be granted to the postal workers:

Last year I recommended
that the minimum and maximum salary should be increased. Speaking from memory, I recommended this year an increase without fixing the amount; I requested the commission to readjust the salaries of the postal workers, postal clerks, and postal porters. I read the reply from the commission the other day in which they said that they did not consider an increase justifiable. I replied to that letter in March, and so far as I know nothing has been done since.

The increase recommended
last year was only $60 per year.

If my memory serves me
rightly I think the amount we recommended would have meant a vote in the estimates amounting to about $260,000.

But the individual increase
would not have been more than $60 per year?

It would likely be around
that figure.

I believe there was some
correspondence tabled this year in relation to that particular question, but I have not had the time to look it up. The minister was good enough to inform the house the other night that he has exerted his very best efforts to obtain an increase for these postal employees, and he also went so far as to say that he had persuaded the government to side with his particular view. When I spoke on this question the other night I expressed some astonishment that the Civil Service Commission had not taken the proper action when the government were so unanimous in their views. It is quite possible that the Civil Service Commission turned it down because the recommendation of the Postmaster General would have meant so little to the men employed in the postal service. I am a very firm believer in the Civil Service Commission, and I would not like to see anything done which would impair the usefulness of that organization. However, the men in the postal department are becoming so disgusted with the actions of the government that they are beginning to ask that the question of salaries be taken out of the jurisdiction of the commission. But we should realize that once we begin to tamper with one of the main functions of that organization it will not be long before the commission will be wiped' out of existence.
The Postmaster General has offered these men an increase of $5 per month. Had his recommendation been carried out it would mean they would receive a minimum of S90 per month. I do not think the Postmaster General or any member of this house will say that $90 per month is a decent living wage. Yesterday the Postmaster General, when making a defence of his department, paid a very eloquent tribute to the men and women employed in the department. He said that they were mostly responsible for the efficiency of the department, and I think the men who give such good service to the government and to the people of this country are deserving of at least a decent living wage. The government has not as yet recognized that fact, except for the recommendation of a $5 per month increase.
I would like to read a letter which is characteristic of a number I have received from

different parts of this country. This is a letter from an ex-service man in the city of Toronto:
I receive as salary $85 per month. Started to work on the city staff in September 1928; received my appointment latter part of February 1929,-
He then goes on to say that out of the salary of $85 per month a deduction of $8.50 is made, leaving a salary of $76.50, which he receives for his services.

What is the deduction
for?

He does not say, but I
imagine that part of it is for superannuation. The letter continues:
I have a wife and eight children to support on my salary, which as you will see is really only $76.50 per month. Would be indebted to you if you would place these facts before the house as I feel sure that were they aware of the small pittance paid to postal helpers, and the hardships caused through same, a large number of whom are returned men like myself, I have confidence to believe that there is not a member in the house who would not be in favour of granting us a living wage.
What is his occupation?
He is a postal helper.

This man, the father of

I want to read from another communication which deals more particularly with the Civil Service Commission and its attitude toward the postal employees. This comes from a very high official of the organization and in his communication to me he represents what I believe to be the overwhelming sentiment of those employed in the Post Office Department. He writes:
. despair of ever getting any measure of justice or equity at the hands of the Civil Service Commission. Letter carriers and other postal employees are becoming disgusted waiting for something that does not materialize, o- nothing has been received under the Civil Service Commission since the act was amended in 1919, but a reduction of $156 in their salaries.
Then he goes on:
When we go to the commission with our grievances they never tell us the same story ""'ice. Four years ago they told us if any increase was given us it would have to be given 
to all the civil service; that the amount would be so large the House of Commons would not vote it. The following year they told us if the government would give them the money they would try and distribute it. What they told us in 1928 you will find on page 2 of our circular letter to members of parliament, dated February IS, 1929. This year they advised our committee not to expect any increase as there were lots of men to be got for what they were receiving now.
In other words, when these men went to the Civil Service Commission this year to ask for an adjustment of their salaries, the reply they received was: "If you are not satisfied with your present condition, there are plenty of men to be obtained for the salaries that you are working for." If that is the way in which the Civil Service Commission handles the employees of the government, it seems to me a change should be made in the personnel of the commission.
The Postmaster General, as I said a moment ago, spoke yesterday in the house of the efficiency of the staff under his control. Nothing is more likely to impair the efficiency of that department than underpaying the men. I do not think any hon. member can expect a man who is working for $85, $90 or even $100 a month to be able to continue to give efficient service. We expect a great deal from those in the employ of the Post Office department. We expect the postmen to be courteous, honest, able to meet the public; we require that they shall be men of good character and physique. They have to go out in all sorts and conditions of weather; yet when the postman comes to our house we can almost tell the time by his knock. It is a sign of ingratitude that in the face of all this talk in parliament of our prosperity and our huge surpluses of revenue over expenditure, we refuse to increase the salaries of hundreds and possibly thousands of men in our employ who find it impossible to live on the wages they receive.
I believe I am not doing the Postmaster General an injustice when I say that he recommended an increase of $5 per month to these men, but I want to see him and the government go a little further than that. The least the government can do is to pay to its ablebodied employees a minimum salary of $100 per month as requested by the postal workers in a memorandum to members of the house.
I feel rather disappointed at the action of the government and even of parliament, that we can find no means of overcoming the obstacle of the Civil Service Commission to giving the postal workers what they are entitled to. If the government were to insert in the estimates a sum *hat would allow these men an in-

Supply-Post Office
crease of approximately $120 to $150 a year, parliament, I feel satisfied, would vote it without a dissenting vote. It appears to me that on the present occasion the reason these men are not getting the increase is that parliament is unanimous in its view. IV hen we all agree on a thing, the men apparently cannot get it.
If there were a little disagreement on the question, it is possible that the postal employees would get the increase. Will the Postmaster General hold out any hope whatever to the lower paid men in the postal service of receiving a proper reward for the services they render to the people of the Dominion?

I wish to say just a few
words along the same lines as the observations of my hon. friend. The hon. member for South Wellington in a few very eloquent remarks dealt with this question. He took up the matter with the minister and, after asking certain questions, found out that there were some 10,000 of the lower paid employees. The wages of many of those men would be under $100 a month. One's sympathy goes out to men of that type, who are toying to play the game, trying to be honest and to be worthy of the confidence of the people of the country in classes of service which demand the greatest amount of confidence and honesty. In my own city, for instance, there is no finer group of men than those employed in the Post Office Department, the letter carriers and other postal employees are a very high type of men. Many of them are, of course, reasonably well paid, but the postal helpers and letter carriers certainly deserve the sympathy of the house. I submit to the minister, in view of what has been pointed out by the last speaker as to the unanimous support which this question usually gets in the house-at least the unanimity of views which prevails with respect to it on this side, whether on the part of the group in the other corner or this group here- that the government will have no difficulty in passing such a resolution. They will receive no opposition from our side, and I am sure, if they bring in any such resolution, they will get no opposition over there. Parliament is the high court of the land. The Civil Service Commission, with all due respect-and I am one of those who support it-is not in control of a question like this. This question can be decided by the high court of parliament, by hon. members sitting in this house, and without taking up further time, I think the minister might well consider carrying out the suggestions of the hon. member for South Wellington and the hon. member for North
Winnipeg in regard to increasing the salaries of the lower paid men. It might be said to me-and I will say it so that somebody else will not-that I was at one time in a position to have dealt with the matter. I doubt if the minister would have said this, but he knows I was not in office long enough to deal with a question of this sort. I could not have dealt with it during an election without being accused of having ulterior motives and he knows what it is to be accused of that. I appeal to the minister's sense of generosity, and to the government generally, to deal with this question from a generous standpoint. I can bespeak the support of all the members on this side, and I know the minister need not worry about his own.

It must not be understood
that the salary of a postal helper who is receiving $1,020 a year is fixed at that; it ranges from that figure to the maximum, which is $1,440.

It takes some years to
attain the maximum.

It increases at the rate of
$60 a year. That is the way the Civil Service Commission regulates the matter The salary of a letter carrier begins at a minimum of $1,080 and increases to $1,440, and the salary of a postal clerk goes from $1,080 to $1,740. When they enter the service they enter at a minimum and after a number of years they reach a maximum which is a fairly good wage. My endeavour at the beginning was to increase the minimum and also to increase the maximum. I am not quite sure, but speaking from memory I think I asked that the minimum salary of the postal helper, which is $1,020, be increased by $100, and of course the maximum would also receive that $100 increase. I am speaking from memory, but I think that is about right. I give that information so that the committee will see how the thing works out. The other evening I think I gave the number of employees, namely, letter carriers, 2,710; postal clerks, 3,009; postal helpers, 2,922.

Is it not a fact that if the minister or the government brought in an estimate to increase these salaries, irrespective of anything in the Civil Service Act, parliament is supreme and could carry the matter through?

I think that parliament could, but I cannot lay down a policy for the government in this matter. I would have to have the government state its policy before I could commit myself.

While on this point, may I draw the minister's attention to the fact that in 1919 parliament voted a bonus for the letter carriers of $480, which, with the standard salary of $720, gave them a total of $1,200 as a minimum. Later on there was supposed to be a stabilization of salary to do away with the bonus, and it was understood that this stabilization would not lower the minimum to this class of workers, as to others, but when parliament did stabilize salaries, the result was that instead of receiving a bonus and salary which amounted to $1,200, the letter carriers received a salary of only $1,020.
Going back to the old minimum.
The old minimum was $720.
That is right.

The government did away with the $480 bonus and fixed the minimum salary at $1,020, with no bonus, making a loss of $180 per annum. The point I am making is that the letter carriers actually suffered a loss of $180 a year in the so-called stabilization.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Only as respects the minimum.

It is the minimum we are speaking of, and this is the class that is suffering. It is all very well to say that there has been an increase of $60 a year, but with that increase it would take the letter carrier three years before he would reach the $1,200 which he was receiving before the stabilization.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: It affected very few in the service.
I would not think so; there is quite a number. The suggestion has been made to fix the minimum at $1,200 a year, it strikes me as a reasonable request.

I am sure that the sentiment expressed by the hon. member for Fort William a few months ago, that he had every sympathy with the employees of the Post Office Department and stood solidly behind the Civil Service Commission at all times, except when he was a member of the shadow government-
I deny absolutely that I ever interfered at any time with the Civil Service Commission.
You deny it absolutely?
Absolutely.
You deny that you ever sent telegrams which secured the dismissal of post office officials in any part of Canada?
I deny absolutely that I ever interfered with anybody who was under the Civil Service Commission and that I ever appointed anjHbody who should have been appointed by the Civil Service Commission.

So far as the expressions of sympathy which we have just heard for the poorly paid class of piiblic officials are concerned, more particularly postal-workers, I have every sympathy with the condition of those who are receiving salaries which do not enable them to sustain themselves and their families in that degree of comfort which we as citizens of this country would all like to see. But, sir, it has been a surprise to me during the four sessions I have sat in this house to observe the salience which has been kept respecting the returns of those who are the real wealth producers of this country. What is the situation? The real wealth producers of this country, in the first place, are the agriculturists, the artisans, mechanics, those who are engaged in the leading industries of this country, and the workingmen of Canada. If you take the year of our highest agricultural production-
Order. The hon. gentleman is getting away from the question.

Am I to be called to order, when these post office estimates are up for discussion and hon. members time after time talk about the poorly paid employees in this and other departments, if I endeavour to make a comparison with other poorly paid workers in this country? I was going to say that in the year 1927, which is the last year for which we have the full figures, and the year of our greatest agricultural production, the total agricultural production in this country amounted to $1,780,000,000. In that estimate is counted twice all the agricultural products which are consumed upon the farm in the production of our live stock and live stock products of every kind. When you subtract that amount from the sum total and divide the remainder among 711,090 farmers, which is the number in this country according to the last census-and that does not take in all the small farmers owning one acre or less -you will find that the gross earnings of each individual farmer and his family were less than $2,200 per annum. When you take into account the annual requirements, the necessary farm expenses), interest on investment, et cetera, I invite anyone in this house or out

of it to show where the average farmer in Canada is earning to-day over $1,190. When we come to the forty leading industries of this country and divide the total wage and salary bill of their employees amongst their number, according to the returns of 1924, we find that the average wage for the individual worker-not for himself, his wife and family-is $1,104.41. The earnings of the hired male servant and	the maid servant on the f'arm
together total $1,103 per annum, so that the average farmer of Canada with his wife and family are only able to earn to-day what his man servant and maid servant are receiving on the average throughout Canada. So when we consider the question of the salaries of our public officials, should not the whole economic system in this country be taken into consideration? Because after all is said and done, the real wealth producere of this country constitute the class upon whom the whole burden in the end must fall. If those who do produce the wealth of the country, are able to retain such a small portion to themselves how under heaven can they afford to pay other people any more?

I think in reading from my notes I made a mistake, in fact I am sure I did in giving the figures for the postal helpers. I gave the maximum as $1,440; it should be $1,320. For letter carriers I gave the maximum as $1,440; it should be $1,500. The other figures are correct.

Are not those
figures even in revised form subject to a diminution of so much per cent by way of compulsory contribution to a superannuation fund?
All employees of the government who come under the Pension Act contribute 5 per cent.

So the net is not the figure the Postmaster General has given.
Mr. VENIOT; I have given the minimum and the maximum. Of course it is understood that 5 per cent is deducted for superannuation.

The minimum is
that much less.

Mr. Chairman, I
think some of us will agree that there is altogether too much truth in what the hon. member for South Huron (Mr. McMillan) has stated. The agricultural people are receiving far less than they should receive, and the employees in industry are also receiving far less than they should receive.
I am one of those who believe that we axe not going to get very much improvement until we have a pretty complete reformation of the system. I would go further than I fancy my hon. friend from South Huron would go, though I do not think this is the time to discuss these other questions. I would rather emphasize the relation between the low paid employees of the government and the higher paid. We very easily secure additions in salary, for instance, in the case of the deputy ministers-perhaps their salaries are not too great; I am not discussing that, but I do say there is a very wide discrepancy between the higher paid and the lower paid officials. Whatever may be true of agriculturists or those engaged in industry generally, we are dealing now with one particular class of government employees and I think we would do well to consider, not this class in relation to some other group outside, but rather the actual requirements of this class having regard to living conditions as they are to-day.
In that connection I would refer to a document which I think has been quoted before in this discussion. It is a memorandum issued by the Amalgamated Civil Servants. I will quote two or three brief paragraphs.
First of all the question is put as to the cost of living to-day, and some figures are cited that were given before the industrial relations committee of this house. The memorandum then proceeds:
For our purpose we have taken the figures from The Labour Gazette, which supplies the cost of a weekly budget of staple foods, fuel, light and rent only. It is stated in the Gazette that to estimate the cost of other necessities it is necessary to increase the cost of this budget by 50 per cent. We do not even go as high as this, merely adding 33-1/3 per cent.
Surely, that is a very, very moderate basis on which to go. The argument is concise:
In 1919 the average cost of living was $22.18 per week, which, plus one-third, amounted to $1,557.81 for the year. Compare this with the $1,312.05 actually received by thousands of civil servants considered to be _ in_ the $1,500 maximum class of to-day. Again, in 1920, living costs for the year were $1,794.50. whilst these civil servants received only $1,593.
That is, taking the very lowest minimum figures as put forth in our own Labour Gazette we find that the maximum figure of the postal workers falls far short of the minimum requirement for decent living.
Now, if we in Canada were living in a period of trade depression there might possibly be some reason for this state of affairs, but we are assured by the Minister of Finance that we are living in a period of very great prosperity, and his budget shows a surplus. I would say that under these condi-
Supply-Post Office

tions there is no excuse for permitting such a situation to continue. Let me read another paragraph from this memorandum:
The average weekly budget over the period 1918-1927 was $21.79, amounting, plus one-third, to $1,510.77, while the average amount actually received by the class of civil servants mentioned was $1,396.11. Thus, these employees have, for ten years, been receiving an average salary less by $114.66, than the average cost of a budget, much less than the cost of a minimum health and decency budget.
So much for the higher paid of the postal helpers. Then comes a very strong plea for the lowest paid employees in the service.
The main point, however, which we desire to stress most strongly is, that there are many civil servants in receipt of an average salary far below even $1,200 per annum.
With an average cost of living existing over a period of ten years amounting to $1,510.77 per annum, surely our request for a $1,200 minimum salary errs only on the side of modesty, and justifies us in once again appealing for and urging your support.
I repeat, this seems to be an eminently modest and reasonable request. Our own statistics show that the very minimum required is over $1,500; all that the civil servants here ask is that no one should be paid less than $1,200.
According to some statistics recently brought down at the request of the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Spencer), there are at the present time civil servants of the male sex getting less than $100 per month, full time, 2,089, and temporary, 1,672. To bring all these people up to the $1,200 a year minimum it would take $64,629. Surely not a tremendous amount when we consider the alleged prosperity of this country and the manner in which we can throw away money for certain purposes. In this same return I find that in the post office there are 624 full time employees, and 686 temporary employees receiving less than $100 a month. It would require only $18,534 to bring these people up to the $1,200 class. This is such a small amount I hardly like to put it forward as a reform in government policy, and yet the government seems determined to refuse to take any action about it.
As I said the other day, it seems to me that the Postmaster General is simply hiding behind the Civil Service Commission. He has asked them for very little-some $5 a month -hardly enough to justify the commission in considering seriously any change. If he had asked for $100 or $200 or $300 a year extra he might be justified and the house would be justified in insisting upon its being granted. But the Postmaster General's request is so small that one hardly can blame the Civil Service Commission for not acceding to it. fMr. Woodsworth.]
An hon. gentleman behind me laughs; apparently he is astonished at this argument. But I repeat that the amount asked for is so very small that it seems to me the Postmaster General is merely seeking an excuse and is not very serious about the matter. If he were at all serious he would force it to an issue.
Again, as I said, it seems to me that the Postmaster General is hiding behind the government; for again to-night he says, "I am not the government, I cannot take action". The other night he refused to come out definitely and say that he would recommend such action to the government. Until we have a statement from the Postmaster General that he is prepared: to recommend substantial increases to the government and that the government is prepared to stand by such recommendation, then we shall have to throw the blame for the lack of these increases upon the Postmaster General himself.

I had not intended taking part in this debate, but I have had correspondence with letter carriers and have asked them confidentially to state their opinion on the matter, I asked them plainly: "Do you think the Postmaster General is making a screen of the Civil Service Commission? Do you think that the Civil Service Commission ought to be disbanded, and would you rather go back to the patronage system? If not, what is your opinion regarding this question?" The answer I got was this:	We do not
know and we are not prepared to say that the Postmaster General is hiding behind the Civil Service Commission, making a smoke screen of it. Nor am I prepared to make that charge either, because I have no evidence touching the matter. The Postmaster General on April 5 did make a statement at the instance of the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Thorson) and we all agreed with the conclusions of hon. gentlemen who had spoken before him. The leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) and members of the opposition agreed with the Postmaster General that there should be a substantial increase in the salaries of these employees. The Postmaster General himself said so. Now the question that presents itself to me is this: Can we formulate some sort of proposal which will solve the problem for this year? It seems to me that the Civil Service Commission themselves cannot be such iron clad people as to be impervious to public opinion and to the opinion expressed on either side of this house. They cannot be individuals of that description unless there is something behind it of which

we do not know. Well, I put this proposition to the Postmaster General-and I am not throwing any insinuations at him. We have all expressed the view that these men deserve an increase in salary, and they themselves have stated their position. They say, "The Postmaster General has admitted that we deserve an increase, but what with the commission not taking action and the Postmaster General, although recommending it not being able to enforce it, we are the sufferers". This is the proposition I put to the Postmaster General: Supposing that he himself nominated a committee from both sides of the house and waited upon the Civil Service Commission and asked for a conference, placing the matter before them in a reasonable light. Let us go down on our knees when we do it.

No; we do not need to
go down on our knees. If they have the power which it is said they have, and if the Postmaster General, as he says, cannot help himself, it is not an unreasonable proposal that such a committee as I suggest should meet with the Civil Service Commission and talk the matter over. Let me make another suggestion to the Postmaster General: If the Civil Service Commission do accede to the request-or if they do not- will the Postmaster General, shall I say, show his sincerity in this matter by calculating what the total increase would amount to and including it in the supplementary estimates, so that it may be available when the Civil Service Commission do comply with the request of the house?

I am glad to
be able to say a few words on behalf of the postal workers of the Dominion. I wish to say frankly that I am in favour of an increase to the lower paid postal workers in Canada. I do not think there is any room for argument in that regard. I am very much pleased also to observe to-night such unanimity of opinion in the house touching the question. During the last few days we have listened to a very lengthy discussion from the other side of the house with referrence to the action of the Postmaster General. And what has been the whole weight of the argument, if you can call it an argument, emanating from that side? It has been this: that if, for example, a postmaster died in this country it would be a crime for the Postmaster General to endeavour in any way to keep the service going by appointing a man temporarily. That is about the substance of the argument we have had from the other side. And what do we find to-night? We have heard the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie), an hon. gentleman for whom I have the highest regard. I am always sorry to see him on the other side because he never looks at home; still, I have a very high regard for him. I was therefore glad to hear him; and I was glad to hear the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Manion) also making a plea. But what did it indicate? The Civil Service Commiss'on, which we have been led to believe was a paragon of perfection, for some unaccountable reason now comprises such scoundrels that they will not do full justice to the postal employees. In other words, when hon. gentlemen opposite for their own purpose wish to use the Civil Service Commission, the commission are the finest type of people in the country; but when it does not suit the purpose of hon. gentlemen opposite to represent the commission in this light then they ignore them. Now I want to ask this question: Who at the present time is running the affairs of this country?
No one.

Is it the Civil
Service Commission or the government? When I find the Postmaster General saying that there was a wish to pay the lower paid postal workers more money but that the commission refused to meet this wish, then I ask myself and this house seriously the question I have just put: Who is running this country at the present time?
Veniot.

Well, let me
say to my hon. friends opposite that if they could show anyone as capable of administration as the Postmaster General they would be very well off. What position do we find ourselves in when, all parties being unanimous in the desire to pay more money to the lower salaried employees, we discover that we are impotent in the matter?
No.
Let the government introduce legislation; that is all that is necessary.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: You would block it.

But what I
want to bring out is this: How is it that so suddenly hon. gentlemen opposite change their opinion regarding the Civil Service Commission? At one time they wish the Civil Service Commission to be in absolute control-

Nat the Civil Service Commission, but the law.

My hon. friend is talking too fast; he will learn more when he is here longer. iAt another time hon. gentlemen opposite, when it suits their purpose, desire to override the authority given that same Civil Service Commission under the law. I tell hon. gentlemen opposite they cannot have it both ways; either they must stick to the law at ah times or they must not do so, and if they ore going to stick to it in one case why not stick to it all the time? I want to say emphatically that so far as I am personally concerned, if this government wishes to pay these postal workers or the employees of any other department larger salaries but cannot do so under the existing law, that law should be changed immediately.
That is what has been suggested.

No, hon. gentlemen opposite are not saying that; at one time they say the Civil Service Commission are paragons of perfection and the next moment they say the recommendation of the Civil Service Commission is not worth considering. I have never heard greater inconsistencies in argument in my life, and I am sure the people of this great country will be thoroughly disgusted with such arguments coming from hon. gentlemen opposite.
About ten years ago I remember when certain postal employees in my city were on strike. We had a public meeting, which I attended and where I did a little speaking, and I said very boldly that I condemned the action of postal workers in going on strike. I also said, however, that since they were paid such very * small salaries, and since they were striking for larger salaries, I was with them 100 per cent. I took that position ten years ago and I am of the same opinion to-night.
Has the Civil Service Commission, under the present Civil Service Act, the power to increase these salaries?
Yes, in my judgment it has the power to do so, but I understood the minister to say the commission will not grant his recommendation.

The commission say it is not justified.

If they are wrong in that opinion are they to bind this parliament? The idea is absurd. That commission is our creature, and we cannot permit to exist a wrong which has been brought to our attention. If there is no division of opinion on the question I should like a good many more hon. members on the other side of the house to get up and support this request for action, then I think we might get somewhere; they would force the government to do what is right by these employees and do it this session. revenue for the carrying on of the affairs of this country. I think every member in the house will admit that our primary industries, those of the farm, forest, mine and fisheries, provide the traffic for the railways.
