speechtext:
They provide a great part oi the revenue of the railway workers, and, with the railway workers and those who are employed in industry, provide the revenue to carry on the affairs of the government.
I am one of those who have great respect for the Civil Service Commission as a means of determining the qualifications for entering the service. I do not say that they are always right but I think they do fairly well under the act parliament has given them to administer. In some places that act limits the scope of the commission in determining who shall get the position, but until parliament has the courage to amend the act-bring it a little nearer if you wish to the British act, and I think that would be much better for Canada-we must put up with the act as it is. The Civil Service Commission in considering the salaries to be paid in one department of the service must take into consideration the salaries paid in other government services.
If the minister has so much confidence in the commission why does he appoint another commission to investigate them?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
In the particular service which the hon. gentleman have been discussing there is a surplus of applications for the positions, notwithstanding the salaries paid. The people who accept those positions know before they enter the service what the salary is going to be; they know what the minimum and the maximum are; they know of the pensions provided for their families. In this particular service there is a large waiting list all the time, but in the technical classes the experience has been that men are being drawn away from the service. Industry is offering them more than the government offers, and that is why this commission of advisers was appointed. I am glad to say that the personnel of the commission has been well received by the country as a whole. Their duty is to look into the relativity of certain salaries paid in the public service of Canada to the remuneration for similar services in the different industries of the country.
It is all very well for my hon. friend, the acting leader of the opposition (Mr. Guthrie) to say that we can put an amount in the estimates to take care of the postal workers, but how is that to be allocated?
(Mr. Robb.]

paid.

Control oi
appointments and control of salaries.

speechtext:
Hon. gentlemen opposite have argued that the Civil Service Commission should rule over the civil 78594-138^
service of this country. Notwithstanding any opinion we may have had about the matter, the act has remained without change. Along with all the other members of the government who were present when the proposition of the Postmaster General was made to increase these salaries, I was agreeable to it, and we asked the Civil Service Commission to consider such an increase. But hon. gentlemen opposite will bear in mind that since this government came into office there have been one or two increases granted to the civil service. In what- manner were the Civil Service Commission asked to revise the salaries of the civil service? They were asked to ascertain the wages paid in similar vocations in industrial and commercial life in this country and to fix the salaries of the civil servants on that basis. I am not going to argue that that was done in its entirety, but I do say that those were the instructions given to the Civil Service Commission when the increases were proposed. The commission did their work and parliament accepted that. The salaries were fixed on that basis and it is assumed, rightly or wrongly, that the civil service are on a parity with similar services in other lines of endeavour throughout the country. That is the basis on which we presume those conclusions were reached.
I for one am in favour of an increase to the postal workers. But this is the surprising thing to me: the acting leader of the opposition stands up in his place to-night and states that all the government, has to do is to insert an item in the estimates to provide for this increase. That would be absolutely unfair. As a reason for not recommending an increase at this time, the Civil Service Commission say that it would make the salaries of the postal employees out of line with those of other classes of civil servants. Nevertheless-hon. gentlemen opposite will ignore all these considerations. It seems to me that if the Civil Service Commission are instructed that the minimum salaries paid in those classes are too low, and to readjust them, that is their business; but in all sincerity I do not think parliament is equipped on every occasion to do work of this character at the request of someone in some particular line. I am not quarrelling with the suggestion of the acting leader of the opposition that perhaps the rural mail carriers or the rural postmasters do not receive enough money. But, parliament in its wisdom having set up a civil service commission for this purpose, having given it all the equipment for making investigation, ascertain-

We have not held up the commission as doing no wrong. We have stood behind the Civil Service Act as the governing act over the civil service of this country, and we still stand behind it.
Here is the situation that has arisen in regard to the rate of salary paid to the lower paid classes of the service. The Postmaster General told us last year, and I think he told us again this year, that he had made a recommendation to the Civil Service Commission and that the Civil Service Commission-he will correct me if I am wrong-turned down his request on the ground, at least this was one of the grounds, that if they increased the salaries of the lower paid members of the Post Office Department it would necessarily follow that they would have to increase the salaries paid in connection with similar lines of work in other departments.
That would rather be the inference.

Frankly, that has no
terrors for me. The point at issue is this: Are these men whose position we are now discussing-I would remind the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) that we are now discussing the post office estimates, by the way-paid a sufficient salary? There is unanimity of opinion, or there was until the Minister of Finance spoke, that they are not paid a sufficient salary. If there are other civil servants doing a similar class of work in other departments the same reasoning naturally will apply to their case. We have said-my hon. friend from South Wellington so stated a moment ago-that it was within

(he power of parliament to adjust this matter, and I suggest to the minister and to the government a way in which it could be done, supplementing what my hon. friend from South Wellington said a moment ago. We could take into consideration the question of a minimum salary-a minimum wage, we will put it that way. The suggestion, has been made-I made it myself a few weeks ago- that we should fix S100 a month as the minimum wage for an adult civil servant; that, of course, would not apply to youngsters just entering the sendee as messengers or something of that sort. Let adult civil servants, doing the normal work of an adult, be paid a minimum salary of $100 per month. Some classes might properly be exempted; there would not be very many, and they could be specified. That is a reasonable proposition, and if parliament would so declare the Civil Service Commission would undoubtedly immediately comply. If is within the competence of parliament so to declare.
I pointed out to the minister a few moments ag0-I did it a week ago, and I am going to do it now, and draw it to the attention of the Minister of the Interior as well-that as a matter of fact certain .members of the Post Office Department are to-day receiving less salary than they were in 1919. The facts are clear; there is no escape from them. In 1919 there was a minimum wage to a letter carrier of $720, and there was a bonus paid of $480, making a total of $1,200. The civil service properly asked that the salary be stabilized at that rate as a minimum, and that certain increases then be given. Parliament accordingly fixed the mimimum salary for a letter carrier at $1,200, overriding, if you please, the Civil Service Commission, or disregarding it, in so far as the Civil Service Act is concerned. Parliament did that as a matter of fairness to the underpaid civil servants. They had asked that that rate be stabilized as a minimum salary, and it was virtually agreed that it should be so stabilized. But when action had been taken, this is what resulted: The minimum salary was fixed at $1,020, with no bonus, so that the letter carrier who in 1919 was drawing $720 in salary and $480 as a bonus, or a total of $4,200, finds himself $180 a year or $15 a month, poorer, because he is receiving $1,020 instead of $1,200. There is no excuse for that.

He now receives a maximum salary of $1,500, or a reduction of $156. There is a legitimate grievance which these men have. They find themselves poorer owing to the action of this house in 1924 than they were in 1919. The Postmaster General disclaims responsibility because he says that he cannot act in this matter alone. Very good; then I submit to the government that the situation is such that it ought to engage their attention and be righted this session; it should not be allowed to continue as at present. I brought this matter to the attention of the house last year, as did my hon. friends from Winnipeg; we have it up again this year; there is a general feeling in the house that some action should be taken, yet we simply drift along. It will not do for the government to answer that the Civil Service Commission-
Does my hon. friend suggest that the minimum salary on entrance to the service be $100 pier month?
I suggest a minimum salary of $100 to an adult for the normal work of an adult.

The grievance of some of these employees is that they not only failed to get that accomplished, but they are actually under a lower rate today than they were at that time. So there is a very strong case for these workers. And when my hon. friend the Minister of Finance brings tMr. C. A. Stewart.]
forward the suggestion that the increase would run into other departments, the answer is a simple one:	If in other departments employees doing a similar class of work are receiving these lower rates of pay, then by all means bring them up to the level we are now advocating for the letter carriers and postal workers.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to say
a few words on behalf of the rural counties. We, who represent the farming classes, have broad enough views to understand that letter-carriers are entitled to a reasonable remuneration, in order that they may give to their children a decent education. The hon. member for Vancouver Centre stated that he was in favour of a minimum salary of $100 per month for civil servants. If he is sincere, he also desires that this minimum salary be applicable not only to civil servants but also to those employed in basic industries. Evidently, being the champion of large interests, he did not wish to mention this minimum salary for those employed in industries which help in the development of our natural resources.
I recall reading in newspapers that when the house is in session, it entails an expenditure of $30,000 per day to the country. Well, sir, it is unfortunate to note that during the present week we have already spent $200,000. Why? To find out what everybody knows, that the hon. Postmaster General (Mr. Veniot) is the best Postmaster General that we have had for many years past. His dealings were thoroughly investigated and absolutely nothing illegal was found.
Sir, as a representative of a rural riding, I must point out that a great deal of time is devoted, in this House, to the cause of civil servants and very little thought is given to the farming classes. We have farmers who own lands worth seven or eight thousand dollars and are far from earning the minimum salary the hon. member for Vancouver Centre mentioned a short while ago.
If we, on this side of the House, representatives of rural ridings, are in favour of an equitable salary for the civil servants; if we want them to live decently and give a good education to their families, we equally want the hon. members of the opposition to cast their eyes now and then on the farming classes. When we lowered the duties on farm implements, a few years ago, that was rendering a minimum service to the farmers, yet we met opposition which was not to the credit of these same gentlemen who sit opposite to us.

Once more, I do not wish to further waste the time of the House, however, I want to ask the hon. members sitting on your left, sir, to take a greater interest in the farming classes of this country.

I think sometimes, Mr. Chairman, we speak rather prematurely in regard to these matters ; the unanimity which was apparent earlier in the evening does not now exist. We understood at the outset that every member was agreed on this subject, and that the government were absolutely behind the proposal to increase the rate of pay and bring it up to a fair standard. To-night we find that one or two members on the government side are in favour of this increase, "but"-and there they pause and begin to give some reason why the proposal should not be adopted. Finally the Minister of Finance, upon whom will depend in the main the settlement of this question, tells us that the civil service is well paid. Consequently I do not believe that any suggestions we may offer or any pressure we can put upon the Postmaster General will avail in bringing about a settlement of this question.
Until the next general election.

Perhaps. The
Minister of Finance said that the civil servants have a splendid system of superannuation. But as the member for South Renfrew pointed out, that is not at Bill to the credit of the government. We have heard of cases of civil servants paying into the superannuation fund without receiving a cent in return. It is the best kind of industrial insurance that I know of for the benefit of the company-in this case the government. The Minister of Finance also said that in the end the public pays for these increases. Well, I would point out that the postal helpers are employed in distributing the mail in our cities, and it is from these urban centres that most of the profit from the postal service is derived. Therefore if the public pays for increases of this kind I think the request of the postal helpers should reoeive special consideration at the hands of the government. Besides, the government has not sought to reduce the war tax collected in the cities. Therefore the cities may rightly claim that the postal service should receive fair consideration from the Postmaster General.
It has been said that the government increased the salaries of these men. This is disputed, and it has been pointed out by one member that some of the salaries instead of being increased have been reduced under the settlement which the government claim benefited the postal workers. If this contention of these men as would appear, is well-founded, then I think the government should reconsider the case and see to it that they are given the substantial increase which we all understood they were to receive. I do not think the Postmaster General will deny after what has been pointed out by several hon. members to-night that some of these postal workers are not as well off to-day as they were in 1919. In my opinion this has been demonstrated in the course of the discussion, but it appears as if the Postmaster General now perceives it for the first time. Undoubtedly a grievance exists among the lower paid members of the postal service, and the Postmaster General should accede to our request that these men be placed on an equality with the other postal helpera in regard to increased pay. I have pleasure in supporting the proposal, but after listening to the Minister of Finance I am reluctantly forced to the conclusion that our efforts will fail unless they are more strongly supported on the other side of the house than they have been up to the present time.

I wish to add my voice to the demand that has been made for a living wage for the postal workers of this country. It has been a surprise to me for many years now that somehow or other the government expects certain civil servants to exist on a wage which must be far below the living line, while the men who get seven, eight and nine thousand dollars are continually being further considered. This is not as it should be. We like to think that we are living under a democratic form of government. Regarding the words of the Minister of Finance that many of the primary producers are not in any better position, after all, the rate of remuneration at which a man's services may be obtained does not matter; the government should not expect him to work for a wage on which he cannot live decently. Regarding those whom the Minister of Finance also mentioned, those who furnish the revenue of the nation, the new wealth which is added each year, it is quite true that we are guaranteeing the profits of all other classes except those who really create this new wealth. One way in
Supply-Post Office

which the government can help those who are getting only a poor living wage is for them to lower the cost of living. While we are guaranteeing the profits of one class, we are making it impossible for the wages that are paid to meet the cost of living which every other class has to face. Some means must be found to give these people a living wage. Lately I was told that some of the temporary workers in Ottawa are receiving as low as S68 a month. This is far below what a family can live on these days.
The Minister of Finance also mentioned the rural mail carriers as perhaps the most poorly paid in the whole service, and he said the government do not fix the salaries of these carriers. I think they do worse than fix the salaries; they grind them down to the very lowest cent they can do the work for. There is one rural mail route established in my constituency and the tenders have been twice issued for rural mail carriers; but the price has been too high in each case; yet in each case only a very moderate W'age is asked for the day's work. Moreover, we expect in the rural mail service men who will comply with all the regulations, men who have to be out in all sorts of weather, travelling over all kinds of roads. And we also exact from the rural mail carrier a bond which is not asked for in the case of the city worker. A good deal of consideration is therefore due the rural mail carrier and I should like to see him receive better treatment than he has been getting in the past. Very few of these people get anything like a wage commensurate with the expenses involved in their calling.

I feel constrained to say a word or two in reply to the remarks made this evening by the Minister of Finance. The hon. gentleman asked why we were discussing only postal employees. I am quite prepared to deal with the whole question of wages of all civil servants when the proper time comes; but we are now dealing with post office estimates, hence the discussion of the salaries of postal employees.
As has been already pointed out, in previous years there has been a fairly unanimous feeling in this house in favour of an increase in salary for these men, but so far it has been denied them, let us say, by the Civil Service Commission. Another reason why we should deal with the postal department is that it is one of the revenue producing branches of government; it is the service for which the people pay. I am satisfied, therefore, that the majority of the people do not want to see the postal employees poorly paid; I believe that the people who come into contact with 
the postal service are anxious to see that these employees get a reasonably fair wage for the services they perform.
When the Minister of Finance discussed the question of technical employees and the salaries paid them, he came out with what is to me a most remarkable statement. He said that as there was a shortage of technical employees it was necessary to consider the question of giving to these people an increase in salary. But what did the Minister of Finance actually do? When the Civil Service Commission recomended a fairly large increase in the salaries of these technical employees the minister evidently was dissatisfied with that recomendation and therefore appointed a commission to look into the matter. There is the anomaly, I might say the absurdity of the position in which the Minister of 1' inance finds himself. He went further and made the statement that, so far as these other workers are concerned, these lower paid men, there are too many of this class and consequently we can keep wages down to the absolute minimum. As a labour representative in this house I strongly resent, and I wish to say that the labour movement throughout the Dominion will equally resent the idea that because there is a waiting list, a large number of men out of work, that is any excuse for the government to reduce wages. And that is the only conclusion one can come to from the remarks of the Minister of Finance to-night. He also asked with what particular class of employees the postal workers could be classified. Well, suppose we classify postal employees with the labourers, let us say, of Toronto. The labourers there are paid by the municipal council, I believe, 60 cents per hour, which is probably more than is paid to the postal workers of Toronto. If I were asked with what class of workers I should classify postal employees I should say that the postal worker, in view of the many qualifications which a man must possess in order to become a postman in Canada, and in view of the strict examination he must passs before he enters the public service, ought to be classified at least with policemen and firemen. I have seen the examination test which postal workers are expected to pass before they are accepted, and I venture to say that if the same examination were submitted to members of parliament more than one half of them would not be able to pass it.
Speak for yourself.

I am speaking for myself.
I could not answer half the questions which these people are asked by the Civil Service

Supply-Post Office
Commission to answer. As I say, I would classify the postal workers with at least policemen and firemen, who are receiving more than $85 a month to begin with. I do not know what the salaries of these employees are in different parts of the Dominion, but I know that in Winnipeg they start with 8120 a month. The minimum of that class in Winnipeg to-day is equal to if not greater than the maximum of the postal employees. And, as I have pointed out, the postal employee is expected to pass a very difficult examination.
I resent the implication of the Minister of Finance that wages are to be determined by this government on the principle of supply and demand, that is, that if there are a great number of applicants for positions as postal workers, the salaries of these men must be kept down to the utmost minimum. The minister will not contend that the salary of $85 a month being paid to-day is anything like a reasonable salary for the services these men perform; all he can say is that the salary is commensurate with that paid other workers, and because there are large numbers on the waiting list he says these men are not entitled to any increases. That is something we strongly resent, and personally I think that in his more calm and reflective moments the Minister of Finance would not have made such an assertion.

I had no intention of taking part in this discussion, but I do not think the hon. member is drawing a fair conclusion from the remarks of the Minister of Finance. The Minister of Finance compared these wages with the amounts paid in other lines of work, and said that apparently people were more anxious to enter the employment of the government than to work for private firms. He did not say that because of the large number on the waiting list the wages were being kept down.
I listened with a great deal of interest to the remarks of the acting leader of the opposition to-night, and I quite agree that in the lower classes of the government services the salaries are too small. If a general increase for the lower classes of employees were suggested I should be only too glad to support such a measure. I know of one woman who is attempting to support her mother and keep a small apartment on $60 a month, and I know she has a very hard time of it. I should like to see the salaries of the lower classes in all departments increased.

I have no doubt that the postal workers of Canada will be very glad and thankful for the sympathy of the minister,
but they would be more thankful if he would carry his sympathy to a practical point and induce his colleagues in the government to do something this session. I think my friend the minister will realize what I mean if, when he goes home to-night, he will read the second chapter of the Epistle of St. James.
Now I would like to direct a question to the Postmaster General. Has anything been done recently in connection with an examination called a sortation test in city post offices. Information has come to me in the shape of a telegram to the effect that men who have reached their maximum in the postal service, who have been in the department a long time and who are entitled to full pay, are now being subjected to an annual sortation test under the threat made by public notice, I understand given by the postmaster of Montreal, that unless these men are able to pass this sortation test their salaries will be decreased and they will be degraded in rank. Perhaps I had better read the notice, which was posted in the Montreal office and which is contained in a telegram sent me by the United Postal Workers of Canada, Montreal branch:
Sortation Test
The department has called our attention to the fact that a number of postal _ clerks at Montreal who have reached the maximum rate of pay failed in their case examinations. We are in consequence directed to remind all concerned that clerks must take the test successfully every year, firstly to qualify for the annual increase up to a maximum and then to retain this maximum rate after they have reached it. The official communication adds that unless all these who are drawing maximum pay take the tests successfully in the near future and continue to do so from year to year thereafter the question of reducing their salaries to the next lower grade will be seriously considered. It is up to these concerned to take the warning and to make a serious effort to pass the case examinations successfully if they would save _ themselves the serious consequences of a reduction of salary.
V. Gaudet,
Postmaster.
I want to ask the Postmaster General 'f there is any authority for posting a notice of that kind in the Montreal office.

I think that was done all over Canada. When these men reach their maximum they continue to take their case examination, which is a major examination, and if they fail they are given another year in which to study and practise in order to bring themselves to the point of efficiency required of an official or mail sorter who has reached his maximum and wishes to retain his position. This is done more as a dis-ciplinarj' measure than anything else, in or-

der to try to maintain the efficiency of the service; because if sortation efficiency is allowed to go down the whole organization in that branch is disrupted. I think that practice has been followed in the larger offices all over Canada for years; it is nothing new.

I am glad to have this explanation from the minister. Perhaps he will explain another matter which I desire to bring to his attention. This question is contained in a letter from a prominent citizen of Montreal, written on April 19:
We certainly have a grievance here in Montreal, as I am sure no city in the world of its size and importance has such poor service. Some time ago an English merchant who had spent twenty years in China said of the post office service here that no city in China of half the size would stand it.	I spent the
month of .July last year in Lee, which is a suburb of London, England, twelve miles from Charing Cross but in London. There we had four deliveries in the day, at 7 a.m., 11 a.m., 4 P-m., and 9 p.m. Here in Montreal, just west of W estmount, we have two, one at from 10.30 to 12 a.m. and another between 4 and 5, one delivery on Saturday and none on holidays. If a letter is mailed in any part of Montreal to any other part, no matter how early in the day it is mailed, it will be cause for rejoicing if it gets to its destination the next day, but the chances will be against it. I mailed a letter in London at ten o'clock at night and the recipient called me on the 'phone before 8 a.m. the next morning.
You can do that in Montreal also.

I am bringing this matter to the attention not of the hon. member for Quebec South but of the Postmaster General, ir. the hope that in some way he may be able to remedy conditions, because from this letter it is evident that a grievance exists in that city.

The question has been raised ay the hon. member for Vancouver Centre is to the effect of the stabilization act of 1924. What happened in that connection was that the S480 cost of living bonus had been gradually in part absorbed in increases in salary, and the complaint of the postal men is that when salaries were finally stabilized at least one class was left worse off to the extent ot $156 per annum as compared with what they received before the stabilization took place.
Would that be the class going in?

That may not have been the class going in, although they undoubtedly suffer to the extent of at least $180, the difference between the old total of $1,200 and the amount of $1,020 received after stabilization. If I might make a suggestion to 
the Postmaster General, he might acquaint the house with the particulars of the distribution of that bonus and the result in the end. I am sure he can readily find that information in his office and I believe the house would like to obtain it. The complaint seems thoroughly justified. I have had the opportunity of going into the figures and I find that men are receiving $156 a year less than they received before the stabilization took place. It may be said that the cost of living bonus was not required in 1924 so much as in 1919, but I am not at all sure of that. I do not think the budgets issued by the Minister of Labour will show that the cost of living has decreased to such an extent as to justify the lower pay which the postal men now receive. They require very special qualifications. As the hon. member for North Winnipeg has just said, their duties are extremely onerous; they carry registered mail, collect money, sell stamps, and have other responsibilities which the postal carrier of old did rot have to assume. The ordinary labourer working for the corporation of the city of Toronto-I hope the committee will forgive me for referring to this, but it is something I happen to know something about 

the man who works in the ditches for the city of Toronto gets $1,497 per year for a forty-eight hour week, and he also gets a fortnight's annual holidays.
How much per hour?
He gets $28.80 per week.
Is he a permanent employee?

He is a permanent employee. Every employee who is taken on by the city of Toronto receives sixty cents for every hour he works, and is generally taken on for two, three or four months. His pay for a week amounts to $28.80, or $1,497 per year, with Saturday afternons off and a holiday of two weeks in each year. The men in the postal service deserve at least equal treatment.
As I ventured to say the other night, the government of Canada should make of itself a model employer. I do not mean to say that it should pay exorbitant wages, but it should see that any adult in its employ, possibly a married man with' a family, should not be paid less than is required to keep himself and his family. Hon. members on the opposite side of the house must realize that the present minimum rate will not keep a man, let alone a man with a family.
I understand that the Minister of Finance agreed with the Postmaster General in for-

warding the recommendation of the government to the Civil Service Commission for an increase in the salary of the postal workers.
I can hardly understand the minister's action after hearing him speak to-night, because one can only gather from his remarks that he is opposed to this increase. The Minister of the Interior is also opposed to the increase and takes refuge behind the Civil Service Act. As the hon. member for North Winnipeg has said, the Civil Service Commission recommended an increase in technical salaries which was much higher than the government wished to pay. The Minister of Finance then instituted a commission to inquire into and report on the matter. What is to become of that commission's report if it is to the effect that the government is right in refusing the scale of wages adopted by the Civil Service Commission? I suppose nothing will be done. What is the government going to do if the report is that the scale suggested by the Civil Service Commission is right? After appointing a commission at considerable expense and wasting a lot of time, is the government simply going to treat the report as waste paper unless it happens to meet with its own view? No government should send a commission out on an inquiry having determined ahead of time that if its report be at variance with the government's wishes it will be treated as a nullity. The result logically will be the overriding of the Civil Service Commission, should the report agree with the government's views, and there is no difference in principle between overriding it in that way and increasing the salaries or providing the money with which the increases could be paid.
From the statements of the Postmaster General, the Minister of the Interior and the Minister of Finance it is hard to tell just what is the government's position. Does it intend to and does it wish to increase the wages of these men, or does it intend to leave them as they are? After listening to the hon. member for South Wellington the Postmaster General will surely regard him as an ally. I believe the Postmaster General wants to take this action, and the hon. member for South Wellington has pointed out a way in which it can be done. Parliament stands supreme over any creature of its own, and it can bring legislation down during this session to enable a higher salary to be paid to these employees. If that legislation includes an increase of salary to employees in other departments who are underpaid, then I say that this house will welcome the opportunity to remedy any injustice which may exist in other departments as well as that which does exist in this particular branch of the service.

I have been rather
surprised to-night at the remarks of the various ministers who have spoken upon this question. I think we must all agree that there is something behind this thing which does not appear on the surface. If we trace the whole matter back to the beginning we will find that the government has not been at all fair with the civil servants of Canada. As far as I can see they have been put off from time to time with promises made at election times, and have been more or less deceived by promises made after elections which have not been carried out. The Minister of the Interior said to-night that recommendations had been made for increases in other departments. That statement was made in reply to a question which I asked him. My question was: Did any of the other ministers of the government make similar recommendations to that made by the Postmaster General? I gathered from what he said that such had been the case, that other ministers had made similar recommendations. The Minister of the Interior spoke for all the ministers who were present at the time he was speaking, and he said that they had all been in favour of the increases recommended by the Postmaster General.- I think I am safe in saying that would mean that the majority of the council were in favour of that recommendation. Following up the line taken by the Minister of the Interior, I presume the whole council were in favour of the recommendations which had been made by other ministers of the crown for increases in their departments.
I have been brought into fairly close touch with employees of the government through the New Westminster branch of the Amalgamated Civil Servants of Canada, and I have met a great many of the employees of the various departments. So far as I can see these men are very reasonable in their demands. From time to time they have placed their case before the government, and I think they have done it in an intelligent and reasonable manner, but their representations have not received proper consideration. I agree with the Minister of Finance when he says that there are other departments in which the employees are not being paid enough. I have been informed of complaints of employees of the Public Works department, of penitentiary guards, who are connected with the department of the Minister of Justice; of employees of the departments of National Revenue and Marine and Fisheries, of employees of other departments of the government. I think I could easily demonstrate tonight that in all those departments there are
Supply-Post Office

employees who are much underpaid. I do not think it is fair to say to them, as has been said by the government in many cases: If you do not like the job, then you can resign and let somebody else have it; there are many men looking for your jobs. I do not think that is a fair way of looking at the matter, more particularly in view of the provisions of the Superannuation Act and the conditions attached to the retirement allowance of which the Minister of Finance seems to be so proud. As a matter of fact, under the law as it now stands, if a civil servant who has not been in the employ of the government for at least ten years retires, he gets back none of the money that has been taken monthly from his wages during the time of his employment. I understand that 5 per cent is taken off their wages, and if they leave voluntarily before the ten years expire, they get back not one cent of that money. That is nothing short of brigandage, because it is their money which has been retained, and when they leave the service they are entitled to receive it. The government says:	Yes, you can quit. But
what will the government do? It will confiscate the money of those employees and add it to the enormous balance, running into millions of dollars, which stands to the credit of the government in the retirement fund. That is certainly not fair, reasonable or just. The hon. member for Saskatoon will, I think, agree with me in regard to that. He knows something of the Saskatchewan act, and I think if the government compares the Saskatchewan act with the Dominion act, it will find that the Dominion act is not as fair to employees as the Saskatchewan act. Under the latter act a man has to pay in 4 per cent, not 5 per cent, of his wages, and he can get back the amount standing to his credit whether he retires within ten years or after a longer period. Moreover, he is allowed a better rate of interest than is allowed under the Dominion act.
Saskatchewan is a model for most of the other provinces.

In this connection I would hold it out to the government as an example which might be followed, and I am sure the civil servants in my constituency would be very much pleased if the Saskatchewan act were adopted by the Dominion government. What I am contending is that it is very unfair to say to these men: If you are not satisfied with the wages you are receiving, then you can retire. They are entitled to more reasonable treatment than that.
It is very strange and unfair for the Postmaster General and the other ministers to try

to put the blame on the Civil Service Commission, because they know perfectly well that the blame should not be attached to the commission at all. The government is responsible. If the government carried out one-half of the promises which were made by the ministers during the election, then the civd servants would have no cause to complain.
I have spoken about the penitentiaries, and I wouid point out in that connection that the employees in the penitentiaries are under another disadvantage; that is that .they are not allowed to organize. They do not now belong to the amalgamated civil Servants' association, and they are not permitted to belong to it, because a ruling has been handed down by the Minister of Justice to the effect that they must not join such an organization. As a matter of fact they did at one time belong to it, but later on they were compelled to withdraw and now they are kept out of the organization notwithstanding the statement which has been made recently by the Minister of Labour that the government allows all civil servants to belong to associations and to organize if they so desire.
I believe, as I have stated before, that the civil servants have been unfairly treated by the government. I have seen the requests made by the Amalgamated Civil Servants of Canada, and I say without hesitation that I would support those requests almost- in their entirety. The government must be either deceptive or very weak-kneed. There is something wrong somewhere, and I do not believe this matter will ever be remedied until we get into office a government which will take hold of the matter in a fair and reasonable way, and settle it to the satisfaction not only of the employees themselves, but of the country at large; because I do not believe that the people are anxious that their employees should be asked to work for anything less than a reasonable living wage.
In reference to the particular department which is under review at the present time, it is admitted by the Postmaster General that certain employees are not getting enough and he has recommended an increase. What defence can there be for this flimsy excuse which has been put up by various ministers that under the Civil Service Act it is not within ihe power of the government to take action? We have seen it demonstrated time after time that the Postmaster General or some other minister could and did override the Civil Service Commission.

Does the hon. member approve that?

I say that the government is playing with the Civil Service Commission. There is not one minister who will from his place in the house say honestly and sincerely that he believes in the Civil Service Commission, and there are very few members on that side of the house who will support it. They want to get back to the old patronage system. I have no doubt they will tell you that privately; indeed, they will say it publicly, and they have declared so publicly many times in the house. Why has the government not the courage of its convictions? Why does it not attempt to do away with the Civil Service Commission? The answer is obvious: It is afraid to do so. It is afraid of what the people of the country will say to it at the next election if it adopts a course of that kind. If the hon. member for Saskatoon wants to know, I am and always have been in favour of the Civil Service Commission. I never had patronage and I do not want- it. I think that the patronage can be and is much better administered by the Civil Service Commission than it would be if members on the other side of the house were administering it themselves. I do not believe in this policy of blaming the Civil Service Commission. If the Postmaster General is actually in favour of increasing the wages of these employees, let him stand up and say: I ask for no quarter and I give no quarter to my colleagues in the cabinet. That is what he should do. He is a man of great courage; he has shown that here, and I think it is really disgraceful for him to remain a minister of the crown when his recommendations are not accepted by the government. He can never make me believe, no minister of the orown can make me believe, that the cabinet as a whole is desirous of increasing the *wages of these men at this time. I never will believe it, because if they felt that way about it they would see that the wages were raised in very short order. I suggest to the Postmaster General that he show in the cabinet some of that courage which he has displayed throughout the course of this debate and that he insist on his recommendations being carried out so that these men may be given a fair
deal; and I suggest also that his colleagues take up the question of wages in their respective departments and see that their recommendations for increases are carried out.

Perhaps the minister would explain it.

Yes, and the maple leaf, the Canadian emblem.

I do not know that I can
explain it. Our experts have advised us, perhaps not in connection with this particular matter, but in connection with other matters, that under the system of heraldry the head of the reigning sovereign was a sufficient indication of our connection with the British crown. That is the only reason I can see at the moment. I know that the stamp used to contain a portrait of the sovereign, with the crown.

It is not the crown on
the head to which my hon. friend refers, but the two small crowns in the upper corner of the stamp.

I could not say positively,
but I do not remember any change in that
respect having been made since my time.

General will tell the house what the position of the postal workers is at the present time, and if there is any hope of their getting any increase in salary.

The hon. gentleman is certainly putting a difficult question to me, asking me to reply on behalf of the whole house. Surely he is not sincere when he asks me to state what this house is going to do or what it might do. I have stated my own position in connection with this matter. I have made an honest statement, and I have been sincere in what I have done. The government was also sincere in accepting my recommendation. I am not going into the details of the argument, because I think we have argued it long enough, but I say that it becomes now a matter of policy as to what shall be done and, of course, it is for the government to decide what that policy shall be. Surely the minister does

I do the best I can, but

We do not expect an
answer to any unreasonable question, but what we do expect is this. After accepting the minister's statement of last year as a truthful statement, as he says, of his position, and we give him credit for that, the house at large has discussed this question very fully since, and has indicated to the minister, and through him to his colleagues in the government, that the house is not satisfied with that position. We say that the finding of the commission-which, by the way, is not precisely what it is represented to be by the government, but we will wave aside technicalities-is not satisfactory. We still believe that there is a justifiable grievance on the part of a large body of the civil servants in this country, and we feel that it is our duty to bring this question to the attention of the government. I think the minister himself will admit that the facts which I brought to his attention half an hour or so ago indicate that there is an obvious difficulty or grievance or injustice which ought to be remedied. The minister can scarcely claim to have discharged his duty fully by simply saying: I am only one minister; I cannot do this thing. The attitude of the Minister of Finance was not by any means what the Postmaster General suggests. The Postmaster General says: I put my case before my colleagues, my colleagues endorsed it, and we sent our united

recommendation to the Civil Service Commission, and they rejected it. The Minister of Finance, however, speaking from his place to-night, spoke rather strongly against this matter.

I think the hon. member
is misinterpreting his statement.

I give the Minister of
Finance credit that he spoke very frankly. He made a rather elaborate argument that this particular class of civil servants were paid more than persons engaged in private work of a similar character. That was his position, in a few words. We are not satisfied with that position. We think the government ought to give some attention to the representations made by parliament. I am a little disappointed by the attitude taken by two or three hon. gentlemen to-night, but in the main the expressions of view have been entirely in support of what the minister says his own position is. It ought to be a more comfortable position than he has been occupying during the last week or two, because he has been subject to rather bitter criticism.
I am always comfortable.
We are now saying to the minister: we are behind you, we want to help you give expression to your view in this particular case.
Beware of the Greeks bearing gifts.

No, I am bringing no gifts If I could I would bring this little gift of justice to these workers. I would give back to them at least what was taken away from them when the salary was stabilized. I think it is a horrible injustice to these people. The suggestion is that they were "gold-bricked"- a little bit unparliamentary, perhaps, but it is very expressive of what took place. These workers trusted the government, they thought they were going to get an adjustment that was favourable, and they now find in one case they are getting $180 a year less, in another case $156 a year less, and so on in varying amounts. It is not fair, it is not just. They have placed their case before us repeatedly.
I myself and others brought it here last year; nothing was done and it went over to this year; we are coming towards the end of the session again, and nothing has been done. We can get nothing from the minister. My hon. friend's question was a fair one. What can the government do? Will the Minister of Finance, will the Minister of Justice, will some other minister tell us? The Minister of

Finance is leading the house; will he say this much, that the ministers will collectively consider this whole question and make some statement to the house next week or within a few days? I can assure the minister-and I think I am speaking for everybody on this side of the house-that we will give the government loyal support in every reasonable effort they may make to remedy these grievances. In the light of that, surely the minister will say that the government will review the question and vouchsafe an answer, say. next Monday or Tuesday. Oh, no.

My friend is rather fond of posing as a man of ultra courage. You must have kissed the Blarney stone recently.

I make that appeal to the Minister of Finance now.

On the evening of April 30, I made some remarks in regard to the post office at Sutton, Quebec, and a member of the Civil Service Commission. Yesterday evening I received from the secretary of the commission a letter which I should like to read to the committee as it involves a certain correction. It reads:
In the course of your remarks in the House of Commons on Tuesday evening on the appointment of a postmaster at Sutton, P.Q., you stated that the file had been held in the office of the Civil Service Commission by Commissioner Tremblay for a period of seven months. Your statement reads as follows:
"I must accept the statement which has been made by the hon. Postmaster General, but I would ask him to search his records and search his mind because I believe when he has done so he will find that he personally is the man who is responsible for this file having been lost in Mr. Tremblay's office for seven months." Commissioner Tremblay has asked me to point out to you that while the file was held for a little over two months in his office, a delay for which he assumes full responsibility, it was not held for seven months, as stated in your

speechtext:

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Before the question with regard to the Pacific cable is answered I might point out that it would come more properly under the third item of this vote. The item we are now considering covers salaries and allowances.
I believe the minister would like to dispose of this question in a general way now.

Yesterday I laid on the table all the files we thought it proper to bring down. There are some secret communications between Great Britain and the other contracting parties concerned with this Pacific cable, including Canada, New Zealand and Australia, which it would not be in the public interest or in the interest of these contracting parties to make public to-day, because all negotiations have not been completed as yet.
Just here let me say that the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) asked for these files some time ago, but it was impossible for me to bring them down until yesterday. In a conversation which I had this morning with the hon. member he stated that he would have preferred to have this matter left over for another day, but while I thought at that time I might be able to do so I would like to go on with it now if possible, if I can do so without seriously inconveniencing the hon. member for North Winnipeg. If, when we have disposed of the question, the hon. member desires any further information I will be only too glad to bring it down.
In the meantime let me present a synopsis of what has taken place. The duplicate Pacific cable between Canada and Australia was placed in operation in November, 1926, and it was expected by the Pacific cable board that owing to the improved facilities there would be an immediate increase in the volume of business and a corresponding increase in the revenue. However, in April, 1927, a beam wireless system was placed iu operation between Great Britain and Australia, the rates charged being approximately one-third less than the cable rates. As a result of the successful operation of the beam wireless about 50 per cent of the Pacific cable traffic between Great Britain and Australia has been taken away from the cable and its revenues have been reduced by approximately half a million dollars a year. Moreover, a beam wireless service has been recently inaugurated between Canada and Australia and it is expected this will substantially reduce the volume of United States traffic which is now passing over the Pacific cable and in

Supply-Post Office
this way still further reduce the revenue of the cable which it is anticipated will be then operating at a deficit.
This seems to vindicate Canada's attitude in opposing the duplication of the cable. Just here, in further explanation I might say that when the contracting parties undertook to duplicate this cable Canada was either not consulted or, if she was consulted, protested. The cable was duplicated in spite of Canada's protest, which was entered at that time by the then Postmaster General, Hon. Charles Murphy. Canada, especially urged that the duplication be at least deferred until the beam wireless was given a trial, but to no avail.
In the circumstances all that remained to be done was to arrive if possible at a working arrangement between the wireless and cable interests. Accordingly in November, 1927, Canada made representations to the partner governments of Great Britain, Australia and New Zealand, urging the immediate appointment of a special committee to consider the commercial policy of the cable, including its relation to the wireless system. Such a committee was endorsed by all contracting parties, but the inquiry was extended by the British government to include the eastward cable route from Great Britain to Australia and the competing wireless, so that it has not been limited to the Pacific cable and competing wireless alone. A special conference was therefore held at London composed of representatives of the governments concerned, namely Great Britain, Canada, the Irish Free State, the Commonwealth of Australia, New Zealand, the Union of South Africa and India, and also a representative of the non-self-governing colonies and protectorates with terms of reference empowering them to examine the situation which has arisen as a result of the competition of the beam wireless with cable service, to report thereon and to make recommendations with a view to a common policy being adopted by the various governments concerned.
Canada nominated Sir Campbell Stuart as its representative at the conference and sent Mr. L. J. Gaboury, Deputy Postmaster General and Mr. C. P. Edwards, director of radio telegraphs, Department of Marine and Fisheries, as advisors. One result of the conference was a merger which was affected between the Eastern and associated telegraph companies and the Marconi Wireless Company of Great Britain. Under the proposed settlement there will be returned to Canada in ca^h an amount substantially equivalent to her outlay on the Pacific cable
iMr. Veniot-l
during the twenty-five years of government control. No future payments on Canada's part will be necessary as would certainly have been the case had a settlement not been reached. Control over the rates will be retained in the interests of the public, this feature having been specially safeguarded during the negotiations. A trans-Canada or all red cable route will be continued with provision for its being taken over by the government in the case of emergency.
That is a short outline of what has taken place. The correspondence which has been tabled includes some further telegrams and the complete report of that conference. The British government has passed an enabling law which has attached to it, perhaps as a schedule, a tentative agreement. I understand that that agreement has not as yet been concurred in but it will be shortly. The question now arises whether it will be necessary for Canada to pass enabling legislation as was passed in Great Britain. I am not quite definite on that point but the matter is now receiving the attention which its importance deserves.

With the treasury board
in Great Britain handling the whole thing.

The fault I have to find in connection with this matter is that at the time it came up the Canadian government did not take it up with the British government in order to stop the duplication of the cable. I have read the papers prepared and the report made by the former Postmaster General and' in the main I agree with his attitude, but I consider that this government slipped in that they attempted to deal entirely with the Pacific cable board instead of going over the head of the board to the real authority. I submit to the Postmaster General and to the members of the-government who had fo deal with the question, that if a representative of the Canadian government was doing something which was objectionable to the British government that government would appeal to the Canadian government and the government here would promptly hold an investigation to ascertain the facts and if the complaint were well founded they would apply the remedy. If the Canadian government had appealed to the British government, as I feel they should have done, this extraordinary thing would not have happened and we would not have had the Pacific cable duplicated in its entirety just a few months before the competition of the beam system reduced its traffic by one-half. That is where I find fault with the government. The present Postmaster General has nothing to do with this, but I say that, in effect, the government did not understand the situation and they appealed to the Pacific cable board instead of appealing to the British government when they found they could not get any satisfaction. If they had taken the matter up properly, this would not.

have happened. In effect, this large sum of money that was spent on the last long duplication of the Pacific cable was practically wasted.
There is one feature with regard to the sale of the cable that, I presume, has been given consideration by everybody, and that is the fact that this link of communication within the empire is now out of the hands of the government; it is no longer under their control. It is quite true there are in the act certain provisions whereby the different governments can bring influence to bear upon the Communications Company, but previously in the war this was a government owned cable and well I remember many meetings of the Pacific cable board during the war and particularly during the early part of it when it was demonstrated what a great asset this sable was to the British commonwealth and the allies in general. This was a cable completely controlled by the allied governments which were at war, and whatever they chose to do they could do in the way of confining the messages to those connected with the war or to those that they considered were the most important. I do not quite see how the Postmaster General could make that statement; after Ml, the man was found not guilty by the jury, and it was not a technicality in the sense of the man being charged under a wrong name or something of that sort. I am not suggesting that the minister may not have had cause for dismissing this man; apparently Kirk had taken some letters on his second delivery in the morning and, finding himself unable to deliver them on that round, put them in another pocket on the bag he carried intending to deliver them in the afternoon. speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: BIGHT OF MARRIED WOMEN TO ESTABLISH DOMICILE
speechtext:
I understand, Mr. Chairman, that this bill was given second reading on division, and that there was opposition to the principle when it was so passed. I was absent at the time, but now I want to register a strong protest against the bill and to dissent from its provisions. I believe that it seeks to enact a principle which is absolutely contrary to British law and British doctrine, and that if enacted into law it will create difficulties and complications, which perhaps have not been foreseen.
When I saw that the bill was being introduced I went to the library to peruse a judgment of the privy council in the case of Cook v. Cook and Attorney General for Alberta, which is referred to in the explanatory notes accompanying the bill. In that case it was decided that the domicile of the husband was the only place of jurisdiction for divorce proceedings. The case will be found at page 751 of the Western Weekly Reports, 1926, and there will be found the following

Divorce Proceedings-Domicile
views by two or three eminent judges of the British Privy Council. Lord Haldane said in Lord Advocate v. Jaffrey:
Since Le Mesnrier v. Le Mesurier .	.	.
nothing short of a full juridical domicil within its jurisdiction can justify a British court in pronouncng a decree of divorce.
And then:
There can be only one real domicil.
And further:
There is no authority for the proposition that the husband and wife can have, while they continue married, distinct domicils .... If it were otherwise .... proceedings for dissolving the status of marriage might be carried through in two jurisdictions, possibly with different results.
Lord Cave said:
I doubt whether the rule as to a wife's domicil following that of her husband is founded only upon her obligation to live with him. It appears to me to be more correct to say that it is a consequence of the union between husband and wife brought about by the marriage tie. . . . The rule is no doubt abrogated by a divorce a vinculo and possibly (although this has not yet been finally decided) by a divorce a mensa et thoro or a judicial separation. . . . (As to a possible exception in a) case where a husband who, having been guilty of desertion or some other matrimonial offence in this country, endeavours to deprive his wife of her remedy by changing his domicil; and there is no doubt authority (which it is not now necessary to examine) for the proposition that in such a case the husband will not he allowed to set up his own wrong as an argument for prejudicing his wife's rights.
Anri Lord Shaw said this:
I must not myself be held as assenting to the view that it has ever yet been decided bylaw that even a judicial separation properly and formally obtained would operate as a change in the so-called, and, in my opinion, very doubtfully named domieilium matrimonii.
I see the greatest difficulty in any invasion of the principle which appears to me to be fundamental-namely, that that unity which the marriage signifies is regulated by one domicil and one domicil only

i.e., that of the husband.
I am quite sure that Lord Watson in Le Mesurier v. Le Mesurier treated the matrimonial domicil as the real domicil and nothing but the real domicil, but considered that as the real domicil of one person-namely, the husband. Much confusion may be caused by the introduction of the idea of there being two domicils of the marriage or two domicils of succession while the marriage tie continues.
In a later pasage Lord Shaw adds:
In the great fundamental issues of status and succession the domicil of the wife is the domicil of the husband until divorce a vinculo matrimonii has been obtained.
If this bill becomes law there will be two domiciles, even before the divorce is granted and while the marriage bond between the two parties still exists. As I have said, even in England and in other British countries where 
the principle of divorce is recognized and where divorce courts function they have never so far accepted the principle which this bill seeks to translate into law.
If we adopt the principle of this bill I see certain difficulties. The effect of the bill on persons residing in Quebec and Ontario, for instance, would be peculiar. Any husband residing in either of these provinces could obtain a divorce only by application to parliament, but the bill would enable his wife, in the cases mentioned, to acquire domicile in any of the provinces where there are divorce courts and to obtain a divorce from him, which divorce would be effective in Ontario and Quebec just as though it had been granted by this parliament. Indeed, as I read the bill, I think it is even wider than that so far as its language goes. It sets no limitation, and it would enable the wife to acquire domicile in any part of the world and to obtain a divorce from her husband which would be recognized as valid in Canada.
I may say that I have no experience in this matter inasmuch as I have not practised law in other provinces where there are divorce courts; but I am told that under the present practice the courts go a long way towards trying to ascertain the facts in any given case, and in cases of desertion the matrimonial domicile has not been changed. It is only in a clear case that they will hold the husband to have changed his domicile so effectively as to defeat the wife's action.
The question of domicile as well as that of nationality and naturalization is one which is very difficult of solution, and there has been no practical scheme to meet all the difficulties which are presented. If the provisions of the present bill were given their full effect the result would be that in some cases two actions for divorce might be pending in relation to the same parties and at the same time, one in one province at the suit of the husband and one in another province at the suit of the wife; and there is the possibility that there would be a race to see which would be tried first. And the same thing would happen before the appeal court if the first judgment were appealed from.
I think we ought to adhere to the old British doctrine, which is also the doctrine of natural law, that there should be only one matrimonial domicile for all purposes. It is not a question, as one hon. member suggested when the bill was before the house for second reading, that now that women _ have equal rights with men we should pass this legislation. It is not a question of equality or

Divorce Proceedings-Domicile
rights; it is a question of one marital tie, of one matrimonial domicile. Whether it be the domicile of the husband or of the wife, I care not; but I contend that so long as the marriage continues, so long as that marriage has not been dissolved, there is but one domicile and there should remain but one domicile for all purposes.
Those who believe in divorce may consider that there are at times deserving cases which at present cannot be relieved by reason of certain difficulties. But to redress possible grievances in a few cases you are apt to create troubles and difficulties in a large number of others; and apart from the principle of divorce itself, to which I am opposed, I am for these reasons opposed to the present bill.

A married woman not separated from bed and board has no other domicile than that of her husband.
Clearly, therefore, the passage of the present bill would be a contravention of provincial rights.

speechtext:
There is a great deal of force in the remarks of the Minister of Justice in regard to this bill, and it does appear that the bill possibly goes too far in the endeavour to provide a remedy for the married woman. The first subsection of section
2 relates to any woman who is judicially or otherwise separate, and living separate and apart from he;' husband. That makes the
bill very broad indeed.

speechtext: I had intended moving that those words "or otherwise" be deleted.

subtopic: BIGHT OF MARRIED WOMEN TO ESTABLISH DOMICILE
speechtext:
Even with that change there is still possibly an objection to that clause. Where a judicial separation has been granted, the parties have chosen the remedy which they desire. They make application to the courts for a judicial separation and when that is granted-or if you go further in the paragraph and take the case of those who have entered into a separation agreement* which would be included within that section as I read it-the parties have agreed between themselves upon the nature of the remedy. So far as I can see, that first paragraph goes too far; I should like to see it eliminated altogether. As to the second section of it, regarding the case of desertion, I believe there-is much merit in the language of the bill in this respect.
The Minister of Justice says that as he understands the situation in the courts the judges are always very careful to bring out all the facts regarding any offence by reason of which divorce is sought and that if possible, presuming the facts warrant it, they will endeavour to find that the matrimonial domicile is the domicile of the parties for the purposes of divorce. I want to give just one illustration of what might happen even if the judges were favourable to accepting the matrimonial domicile. A short time ago my attention was drawn to the case of a couple who were married in Ontario twenty years ago. At the time they were married they intended going to the west; immediately after the wedding they did go west, where they homesteaded and preempted land. Their family of four were bom and raised on that farm. Through some misfortune the husband lost part of his land and subsequently rented land and continued farming for a few more years. One fall he thought he would come back to Ontario to work in the bush during the winter months, which he did, leaving his wife and four children on the farm of a neighbour, where his wife kept house and the children were cared for by the neighbour. The husband did not return in the spring, although during the winter he sent her a very little money from time to time. Later on she found he was living in Ontario with another woman, and the evidence disclosed that children were born to that second union in Ontario. Notwithstanding the fact that
Divorce Proceedings-Domicile

these people married with the intention of going west, and in fact did go west where they took up land and brought up their family, that woman's domicile was in Ontario. The husband deserted her; she was left with these four children to support, and in order to get a divorce it would be necessary for her to come to Ontario and follow the husband in that domicile. Ontario is not so very far away, but supposing her husband had gone to Florida or some place in South America. The situation would be exactly the same; she would have to follow him and would have no right to take action in the west or in Ontario after he left Canada. It is to provide for cases of that kind that the sponsor of this bill has been endeavouring to secure legislation which will do justice to all, and in a case such as I have mentioned I see no danger in changing the law in order to permit a woman to acquire a domicile. In that particular case there would be no more danger than in allowing her to acquire a domicile under a judicial separation or under a separation agreement, which is not legal now. With the elimination of that first subsection I think the bill should go through in order to do justice to people who are placed in the position I have mentioned.

speechtext:
As the bill is drafted I find myself altogether in support of the position taken by the Minister of Justice;
I believe some of us do not know just to what extent this legislation may go. The Minister of Justice instanced a case involving the provinces of Quebec and Ontario, and then he went on to state a case which I believe to be equally appropriate. He pointed out that if this legislation were adopted by this house a married woman could go to Nevada, take up her residence and obtain a divorce upon grounds which are not recognized in any part of Canada; then she could say that she was entitled to choose her domicile and entitled to a divorce on the basis of that domicile under a statute of the Dominion of Canada. A woman could go to Peru or Chile, she could go to Paris, as has been done quite often recently. As this bill is drawn now it does not limit the woman's domicile to Canada and does not provide that she may acquire a domicile for herself within Canada; it allows her to acquire a domicile in any part of the wide world. Those who support this bill should at least provide that after the first line of section 2 should be added the words "living within Canada" and that the words "within Canada" should be added after the word "herself." That would make the bill read as follows: fMr. Both well.1
For the purposes of this act a married woman living within Canada .... may acquire a domicile for herself within Canada. . . .
I have no sympathy with the man who disregards the obligations he took upon himself in contracting marriage, obligations which I am glad to say most Canadians are proud to observe; I do not believe he should be allowed to treat his wife inhumanly, contrary to the law, and then move away and so prevent an action being brought against him. I am in favour of divorce on the statutory ground; when that ground exists I believe divorce is a duty. I know there are others who take a different view, but I do not think divorce should be granted on other than the recognized statutory grounds which obtain in this country at present, so I am not prepared to support anything which will permit a woman to go away and obtain a divorce on other grounds. I believe these people should remain within Canada and have their cases disposed of by a competent court or by the senate.
