Progress reported.
Mail service, including mail service by air. $16,305,000.

As this estimate greatly concerns the constituency which I represent as well as the larger part of northern and central British Columbia, even at the cost of detaining the committee for a short time I feel that the matter is of sufficient importance to justify my speaking on it in the hope of enlisting the sympathy of the Postmaster General and also in order to bring before this house the importance of a good mail service in the isolated parts of Canada. As we all know, efficient mail and telephone service is very important to the settled parts of our country, but it is particularly important to the sparsely settled portions of this Dominion. I do not believe there are two other factons which tend so much to solidify the rural population and to give courage and confidence to the people who are filling up the big spaces which need

Supply-Post Office
population as good mail and telephone services. The greatest handicap that people in the rural districts have to overcome to-day is the lack of an efficient mail and telephone service. As the Postmaster General knows, various requests have been sent to his department, not merely by representatives but by every board of trade sitting individually as a board and by the associated boards of trade from Prince George on the east to Vancouver on the west, a distance of over five hundred miles. After looking through the estimates it seems to me that those that have get more and those that have not geit nothing. I notice that, in the big centres, where there is undoubtedly and necessarily a good service, there is a duplication with an air mail service, but in the places wdiere the greatest need exists we find very often that only a partial or an irregular and uncertain service exists.
I do not intend to offer any criticism which might be considered as adverse to the Postmaster General's department, but I desire to show a picture of the actual conditions which prevail throughout the northern and central parts of British Columbia. There are four methods of handling mail in Canada. The first and latest is the air mail service. I am sure that every member of the house who has listened to the story of the development of the air mail service in Canada during the last few years must look forward with great optimism to the future of this service. The report of the Deputy Postmaster General shows that there is air mail service now to the Magdalen islands and to the island of Anticosti. These places have had a very infrequent mail service in the past but they are now being brought in touch with' the outside world. I regretted very much to hear the Postmaster General say that he did not intend to inaugurate any air mail service this year in British Columbia. I regretted that still more when I read the following words in the report of the Deputy Postmaster General with respect to the air mail service to the Magdalen islands and Anticosti:
Both from a mail service and a humanitarian point of view, the successful operation of such a service it was thought would do much to ameliorate the conditions under which these islanders existed during the winter months.
This service was inaugurated not merely to give them mail communication but also from a humanitarian, point of view. I wonder if the Postmaster General's humanitarian point of view could extend at this moment across the prairie provinces, through the rockies and dip over into British Columbia?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: To Prince Rupert?

The hon. Minister of Justice is quite right, yes, and I will refer to that in a moment. I intend to give the house two or three striking instances by mentioning some districts which have practically no mail service. When I asked a question this afternoon as to the sources of information which the Postmaster General had as to the need for rural mail services, I was pleased indeed to find out how the Postmaster General was notified of the districts where mail service was required. I spent the four and one-half months between the closing of the house last year and the month of November in travelling through my constituency but even though I spent that length of time in practically continuous travelling I was not able to complete the circuit of three-fourths of the country. When I went up the Naas river I found a large settlement of people there and they complained that the mail service had been so infrequent that parcels mailed before Christmas had not reached them until the month of April. I do not directly blame the Postmaster General for that but I do say that as long as the district postal supervisor is - living in Vancouver and is not in touch with the conditions which prevail in the northern part of the country, it is hopeless for me to come here and try to give an accurate description of the conditions which prevail there. When I went to Mill Bay to start up the Naas valley, I hoped to be able to get the little mail boat going from Mill Bay to Aiyansh. If that little boat, which was supposed to take the mail up the river fifty-two miles-and it was a mail day when I reached there-had been in operation and at my disposal, I could have gone up that river for $7.50. The boat was lying at the wharf, but the man who was taking the mail was drunk.
Oh, oh I
What is the date of that?

January 15, 1929. The last time that we took this matter up with the Deputy Postmaster General and we asked that he should, at least on alternate days, put on a baggage service, the reply, after some weeks, was that the cost would be prohibitive. I went to some trouble in order to find out what it would cost to put on a baggage car service three days a week during the summer schedule, and I believe the cost would be nothing like what the dteputy minister said it would be. Furthermore, I think there is a daily mail service from Vancouver down through the Okanagan to Calgary. If any part of British Columbia deserves consideration in the matter of a daily mail service it is the port of Prince Rupert, and the country lying contiguous to it east to Prince George. Why the department has refused to grant that legitimate demand is beyond me. I feel assured that if the Postmaster General realized the great need of this country for a daily mail service he would not fail to see that it was inaugurated this very year. A great number of the people in the east are ignorant of the west. Very few' people that I meet, I am referring particularly to people in the eastern provinces, are aware of the great future and of the splendid strategic position which the port of Prince Rupert occupies on the Pacific coast. I am not speaking to^might in a way that can be construed as having the slightest political tinge, but I do want to bring home to the Postmaster General and his department the fact that outside of Canada the port of Prince Rupert has received very high recognition indeed. Just as in the east we find in Montreal the great -powerful and central lever which dictates and guides to a great extent the movement of commerce, so in the west I

Supply-Post Office
say, even though there may be Vancouver members present here, that Prince Rupert on the Pacific coast has not had a square deal. An elevator was built there, and left lying idle. Vancouver got over eighty million bushels of wheat, and the wheat is going there still, while Prince Rupert got only two million bushels, and then the elevator was closed down.
Who was to blame for that?
Never mind about the blame just now.
Who can remedy it?

That situation can be remedied easily, and I may have a few words to say on this subject when the elevator items are up for discussion. I was saying that Prince Rupert is recognized by outsiders as occupying a strategic position on the Pacific coast as a base for an aeroplane service. In that connection I would like to quote just a few words from Captain McCarthy, the cousin of Captain Kingsford Smith, of the Southern Cross, the famous hero whose deeds in the air have won for him immortal fame. Captain McCarthy, representing the International Airways Company of Seattle, in his biplane made a survey flight from Seattle to Alaska prior to an ambitious air service being inaugurated between Seattle and Alaska. He landed in Prince Rupert on March 18th of this year on his way to Nome, and it is very interesting to note what he had to say of the port of Prince Rupert. Here are his exact words:
In any event air service between Seattle and Alaska or to the Orient, Prince Rupert will through its location have to be a base of call or departure. This port is in a strategic position and will eventually have to be equipped with a radio beacon and other aids to aerial navigation.
He went on to say that Prince Rupert today was fully ripe for an air mail service between Prince Rupert, Telegraph Creek, Atlin, Dawson and Mayo, and every bit of that line would be within Canada. I do not expect after what the Postmaster General has said that we can have that air mail service inaugurated at this time, but the hour will come, and come soon, when such a service must be established. What I am asking the Postmaster General to do is to have a survey made of the conditions that prevail in the great constituency of Skeena, and find out the actual needs for rural mail delivery. I noticed in looking over the returns that have been laid before the house 78594-1411
of applications for rural mail routes, that there has been no demand from the constituency of Skeena. The Postmaster General admits that that is correct? Very good. I went through the whole Skeena country last year, travelling through it for four and a half months, and I want to assure the Postmaster General that the time is ripe in all sections of the Ominica and Skeena country for the inauguration of rural mail delivery. Here is what I saw. 1 saw farmers come in to Smith-ers, a distance of sixteen miles-sixteen miles, mark you-to get their mail at the Smithers post office, and when they reached there, owing to some difficulties with which they met on the way, the post office was closed. They had to wait over the whole of that night or else go home without their mail till the following morning when the post office opened. I am not going to blame the Postmaster General for that because it is quite evident from this report that has been tabled that no recommendations have been made to him for the establishment of rural mail delivery in that country. At Telegraph Creek to-day the mail service is very inadequate. It is very difficult to get a decent mail service in winter. The mail is brought in by dog sled, and from October until June, the people are supposed to get ten deliveries and the maximum that the dogs can haul is 125 pounds weight. What happens very often is that the people do not get anything like that number of deliveries, and what I want to drive home to the Postmaster General to-night is that the time has come when these needs for rural mail delivery in very difficult country must be met in some way. We should at least do for these people what has been done so well for the inhabitants of Anticosti and the Magdalen Islands. To my mind it is much better to be able to guarantee seven deliveries of mail to these people living in these outlying places, seven mails that they are sure of getting, than offering them fifteen deliveries and actually giving them only two or three. The people in the rural districts of Ontario know nothing of the difficulties that beset the people in northern British Columbia. It would be impossible*for them to know what the conditions there are like. It is a young country among the mining camps, the great lumbering camps and fishing places, and the big need of these people is a mail service. I ask the government and the department of the Postmaster General to attack honestly and courageously that problem of giving an efficient mail service wherever the needs of the people demand it. I do not agree with
Supply-Post Office

those who say that the Post Office department should always show a credit balance. Of all the departments of government the Post Office department most intimately affects the well-being and happiness of the people by providing a proper mail service. Whenever we are considering the installation of a mail service we should not say: that is going to cost too much. I think the federal government should follow where the provincial government leads, where the latter constructs roads, opens up land and brings in the people. In such cases I contend that the federal government should follow close behind the provincial government in the matters of mail service and telephone communication.
As regards the geography of Ontario and Quebec, and the maritime provinces, I would not take second place to any man in knowledge of the climate, the conditions, the people, and the resources of those provinces. I should like the same thing to be said regarding the country whence I come. Sir, to reach the Naas valley I had to navigate a river where you took your life in your hands. That river is the only way in and the only way out. Now, sometimes in this house we have a rather poor sense of humour. I used to be very humorous but I have lost all sense of humour since I entered this house. When I am outside in the broad fields, where I can talk to men who are willing to understand, I have no difficulty in telling them a good story; but in the House of Commons it seems to be really futile, and for this reason-oh, I sense it from the psychological standpoint-I know that anything I say by way of pleading is given by hon. members opposite, the political tinge. That is the sad part about our proceedings here. Now, I do not think that of all hon. gentlemen across the way, but I believe there is in this house to-day a spirit broad enough to interpret the wishes of the people. Up in that valley a mother broke her leg in the fields where she was working. The only one who could succour her was her husband. He set her leg. There was no medical aid. She had to endure the agony. Now, I wonder how many hon. members here could do that? What I want to drive home is this: It is all very well for us to be sitting in comfort here; we do not realize what pain is.
We only think we are sitting in comfort. We are not so comfortable.

Oh yes, you are. For two months or more this woman suffered intense pain, for it was impossible to give her medical attention; the nearest doctor would be a little over 150 miles away. She would have had to go down to Prince Rupert, and in her condition the journey was out of the question.
[Mr. Brady.3
You do not blame that on the Postmaster General do you?

No, I am not referring to the Postmaster General. I am just giving the conditions that prevail, to show the necessity of a sympathetic understanding on the part of the government. To the people in these isolated places the government should give a mail service-not a daily service, they do not ask for it, but a good weekly service. I do think that the two most important requirements in western Canada to-day are proper mail service and proper telephone communication.
Now, sir, I am going to ask the Postmaster General one or two questions before taking my seat. First, is there any chance that the wishes of all the people at Skeena as well as of the Cariboo, in which district Prince George is situated, will be met, and that a daily mail service will be inaugurated between Edmonton and Prince Rupert?
The only answer I can give the hon. gentleman now is that this is the first time the case has been placed before me so cleanly, and I will certainly go into it in a serious way.
Thank you, sir. Would the Postmaster General give me the cost of the baggage mail service between. Quebec and Cochrane that was introduced last year?
I could not tell the hon. member offhand, but I could give him the rates we have to pay.
Has not the deputy minister the information?

Perhaps he has the details. We have to pay for baggage car service the following rates: three-feet unit space, four cents per mile; seven-feet unit space, 6.5 cents per mile; fifteen-feet unit space, thirteen cents per mile; thirty-feet unit space, twenty cents per mile. Those rates are regulated by the railway commission.

I have some figures on the subject. I found that we could get a baggage car service three times a week during the summer months at the following rate: seven-feet space from Edmonton to Prince George, serving ,points en route, would cost $45.50 a trip; a. fiftyrfeet space from Prince George to Prince Rupert, $18 a trip. Multiplying the whole thing it would give us a summer schedule of twenty weeks for about $6,109.

I will go into the matter. I should not like to take the hon. gentleman's figures.

Supply-Post Office
I would not expect the minister to do that. I mentioned1 them just to give him an idea.
I shall go into it.
The hon. gentleman's time is up.

Mr. Chairman, there are two or three small items I should: like to clear up.
Some hon MEMBERS: Oh, oh.
I am serious about it-if you do not get too gay.
Order.

At six o'clock the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg, who is not here now, asked for certain information in connection with the tenders for air mail services. On his behalf I want to request that the Postmaster General lay on the table a list of the parties who were asked to tender for these various services, the amounts of their tenders, the names of the successful tenderers, and copies of the contracts. I do not expect that this information can be given to-day, but perhaps it can be brought down soon.
It will take at least three or four days to get that information together, but we will get it.
With reference to the Mackenzie river mail service, what was the volume of mail carried over that route?
I do not know whether I can give that information.
It could be obtained?

I have not the information; I did not expect it would be asked for, but I will get it. I think we can get the poundage. One thing I do know is that considerable mail gathers there, and I know we had to make several trips with 750 to 1,000 pounds of accumulated mail. That gives some idea of what was carried, but we will get that information.
That will be satisfactory later on. When did that, service up the Mackenzie river begin?
During the winter; I think it was around January or December.

Is it still being
carried on?

No, I think it has been
discontinued now; it was only a trial.
Who had the contract for it?
I gave the name this afternoon; I think it was Western Canada Airways.
Does the Department of National Defence provide airplanes in connection with these mails?
No. The Department of National Defence did provide some of their planes in emergencies for eastern services this winter, but only for a short time.

There is one other matter to which the Postmaster General referred upon the request of my leader, who is not here to-night. He requested some information in connection with the complaint of the Commercial Airways Limited and the Great West Airways Limited, that when tenders were asked for the transportation of mail between Winnipeg and Calgary these companies were given no opportunity to submit tenders. The Postmaster General promised he would look into the matter and give the information.

I did give some information and I said I thought Captain McCall was on the way; he had been wired to and had replied he was coming to town to discuss matters with us. He has been here with Mr. Sick and has been in conference with myself for a short time and with the superintendent of air mail services for a considerable time. He was given further specifications required for such services and has left his memo. I did not have an opportunity of discussing it further with him and I understand that both Captain McCall and Mr. Sick have gone home.
Give us the figures allowing the amounts paid the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific Railway for the carriage of mails.

The Canadian National
Railways received $3,133,767.67; the Canadian Pacific Railway, $3,822,983.94, and other railway lines 8481,140.52, making a total of $7,437,892.13 for rail service for mail.
Is there not a discrepancy between the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian National Railway figures when one considers the mileage of the two systems?

What was that?
Supply-Post Office

If I have the figures correctly the Canadian Pacific Railway, with
16,000	miles, gets about $3,800,000, while the Canadian National Railway, with about 20,000 miles, gets about $3,100,000.
What is the reason for that discrepancy?
The only reason I can see for it is that the Canadian National Railways do not give the same mail accommodation.

And is it not clear that
the Canadian Pacific Railway territory has more frequent mail sendee?
No, I do not think so.

That is one of the cases of which we had an illustration to-night in connection with this service between Edmonton and Prince Rupert, as against the service further south on the Canadian Pacific Railway line west of Calgary.
They may have more frequent train connections between those places than on the Canadian National between certain other places; I do not know.
Is preference shown to railway mail clerks in the appointment of district superintendents?

There is no preference
shown.
Is it not a fact that more railway mail clerks than others are selected as district superintendents?

I would not say that. Whenever there is a vacancy it is advertised and railway mail -clerks as well as other permanent employees have a right to contest for the vacancy. Their applications are received, and they go before the rating board, which judges as to their ability, capacity and seniority. They are given examinations each year during a period of years; the results of those examinations are placed before the Civil Service Commission, and their rating decides who geits the position-. There is no other preference at all.
Mr. RO-SS (Kingston): Who compose the rating board?
The district superintendent is a member of the rating board, and in other cases we take mentbers of the board from the head office of the department.
It may be that the district superintendent, in most cases being a former railway mail clerk, does show a preference in the rating.
I would not want to say that; it would be expressing want of faith in the honesty of the officials.
But there is criticism among inside men that they are not getting a show in the matter of these positions.

I have heard the criticism and I have had one or two cases pointed out to me, but I found no ground for such criticism.
M-r. ROSS (Kingston): It does seem that a post office clerk would have more experience than a railway mail clerk for such a position.
Not always.

I would like to
ask what is included in the item of $150,000 for the Yukon Territory. What service does the government get for that amount?
Mr. VENIOTThere is no increase over last year; that amount covers mail service in the Yukon Territory and the salaries of postmasters and staffs of Dawson and White Horse, also telephones, rentals, telegrams and so on. The staff of the Dawson post office consists of one postmaster with a salary of $5,000, plus $900 rent allowance, and three postal clerks. The staff at White Horse consists of one postmaster with a salary of $3,120 and -two postal clerks, one of whom is temporary. The salary range for postal clerks at Dawson is from $2,520 to $2,640. Owing to the unusual conditions existing in the Yukon Territory salary ranges are higher than those in other parts of Canada, and that salary range is approved by the Civil Service Commission. The balance of that amount provides for the transportation of mails.

Does that include
the amount paid the Canadian Pacific Railway Company and the Canadian National Railways -for hauling mail up the west coast of British Columbia and Alaska and into the Yuk-on. They carry the Canadian mails north as well as the Alaskan mail, a large quantity of which goes north through Yukon.

I will- secure that information for my hon. friend.
Mr. SPEAKMA-N:	Under this item I
would like -to direct the attention of the -Postmaster General to a -matter of local service within my own district, at a point

Supply-Post Office
with which I am very familiar. As some of the members of this committee may know, the little city of Red Deer lies midway between Calgary and Edmonton on the C. & E. branch of the Canadian Pacific Railway, and acts as a distribution centre for the settlements in that locality. The service on the Canadian Pacific Railway is excellent; and I have no complaint to make upon that point. Their service with regard to passengers, freight and mail is as good as it possibly could be, but Red Deer is also situated on the Brazeau branch of the Canadian National Railways, the branch running out to Brazeau and terminating at Nordegg. On the west side of Red Deer and on that branch of the Canadian National there are a number of small towns and villages, situated between Red Deer and Nordegg. These villages are provided with a baggage car service from Red Deer west. The small villages east of Red Deer are without that service at the present time; the two villages are Joffre and Haynes. Baggage car service is carried on between Red Deer and Nordegg and that provides for the small towns west of Red Deer, but the towns east of Red Deer situated on the Canadian National Railways are served by rural mail routes running from points on the Canadian Pacific Railway and providing the farmers and the residents of these small towns with mail service. The service is bi-weekly, and it has been felt for some time by the business men and residents of that locality that the service is hardly sufficient to meet the needs of that productive, well settled territory.
I stated that Red Deer formed a distributing point for most of these small villages, and as a matter of fact these places east of Red Deer on the Canadian National railway get most of their supplies from Red Deer. They have found it extremely difficult to carry on business and are greatly handicapped by the fact that any business correspondence eomdng to them from Red Deer or other points must travel north to Lacombe by the Canadian Pacific Railway, and in one case must be transferred to the Stettler line, and from a point on that line the mail is hauled to the villages. The result is that while they can order their goods from Red Deer easily enough the business correspondence in connection with these supplies arrives two and sometimes four days later than the supplies themselves. That situation affects not only the business men in these places where a good deal of business is done,
but also a large number of farmers and settlers who are not upon the present routes, but who get thedr mail at the post offices in these villages.

They are back from the
railway?

Yes. These people request that a baggage car service be given them on the same terms as it is now given to the towns lying west from Red Deer. The Postmaster General is somewhat familiar with the situation, although I do not expect him to carry all the details in his head. However, he has had some correspondence with me in this regard and apparently the difficulty is the additional cost involved, because it is fairly well understood that it would be impossible to discontinue the rural mail routes in favour of the baggage car service. Once you have the rural mail route established it is a difficult thing to take away that service, to which the farmers have become accustomed. So I am not suggesting that that be done, but I do suggest that it would be worth while to give the additional service by rail. I have here an estimate as to the additional cost, provided by the Post Office department. As a result of the proposed change the estimated additional cost would be something like $725 a year, which is considerably more than the revenue derived from these two points at present. However, there is a fact which never had been considered by the department, namely, that we will not get revenue until service is provided, and it is impossible to compute the loss involved or the revenue involved unless the additional business that will be done through the establishment of better service at these points is considered. I have asked the Postmaster General to give this service; I have gone into the matter carefully and my estimate is that the additional revenue wliich will be produced through the sale of stamps, money orders and so on, which cannot now be carried on at these two points, will go a long way towards meeting that suggested deficit. I am not asking the Postmaster General to give me an immediate promise in this connection; I do not think that would be fair to him, because he should have an opportunity of again considering the matter before making any definite announcement. However, I do ask that he again consider establishing this service, taking into account the fact that the districts are old and well settled, and already provide quite a good deal of business and quite a heavy freight tonnage.
Supply-Post Office

I will go into the matter
fully.

I would like to
ask the Postmaster General to give me some particulars in connection with the St. John post office. Ini the list of post offices I notice there is a decrease in the estimate for St. John amounting to SI 1,640. I would like to ask the Postmaster General why this estimate has been reduced.

Mr. BLAjCK (Yukon):	Would the Postmaster General be good enough to inform the house if the total vote of $150,000 for the Yukon territory is required for mail service?

Just a portion of that vote is required for mail service. The main service in the Yukon is the winter service from White Horse to Dawson which is arranged for by the tender and contract system. The summer service is a monopoly, the British Yukon Navigation Company being the only company operating boats. The other services are quite small and are arranged for from year to year.

I know of no transportation costs which are paid to the Canadian National or to the Canadian Pacific Railway in connection with that service.

I notice that the
Postmaster General is now calling for tenders for the winter mail contract, the present contract expiring at the beginning of navigation this year. It is rather disappointing to see that a better service is not being contemplated. I think we should get a better service for the money which is paid, a rather generous amount for this winter mail service. The route covers about four hundred miles, with a branch line of eighty miles, and the contract provides for a weekly delivery of mail each way between railhead at White Horse and Dawson, the northern extremity of the route. During the broken period between the closing of navigation and the opening up of winter travel the contractor is only required to haul 1,200 pounds per week. During the winter period he is obliged to haul 2,500 pounds per week and under the regulations the contractor is obliged to haul merchandise paying first class mail rates in preference to newspapers and reading matter. The consequence is that the mails are cluttered up with tons of merchandise and the newspapers and periodicals are left at railhead and accumulate there all winter until there is almost a boatload of them in the spring, when they are not worth moving. I think that should be remedied by allowing merchandise to go forward to railhead at parcel post rates and it could be hauled into the interior at freight rates that would cost the consignees less than the present rates and would not congest the mails. I think the contract for the future should require that more tonnage be hauled per week.
I am glad the hon. member has drawn my attention to that; I will go into the matter immediately.

I bel icve you
should ask for more than 2,500 pounds per week. I notice that the specifications permit the contractor to haul the mail by aeroplane. The present contractors have been enterprising enough to install an aeroplane service and they are hauling the mail by that means without any extra cost to the government.
I do not think that has occurred anywhere else in Canada.

They asked for that permission some four months ago and we granted it to them, saying that it did not make any difference to us how they got the mail in.

Supply-Post Office

I should be glad if at some time the Postmaster General would give the house a concise statement of what the air mail service has cost the Dominion of Canada to the present date, and what revenue we are deriving from it. This matter of " keeping up with-the Joneses " and trying to have an air mail service equal to that of a country with a population of 120,000,000, is very fine, but I have to struggle to get mail boxes for a few farmers and I cannot get them on account of the cost, while at the same time we are placing an item of $800,000 additional in the estimates for a play-toy running between Toronto and Montreal which the Postmaster General says very few appreciate and very few are patronizing. I would plead with the Postmaster General to get away from the big interests and the moneyed classes and get his ear to the ground. Let him listen to those in the far-flung parts of Canada and to bona fide farmers who have to go a mile or a mile and a tenth for their mail. Let him get down and serve the masses before he spends millions more each year in the interests of the classes, and in trying to "keep up with the Joneses" with this play-toy, the air-mail service. I want to bring to the notice of the Postmaster General the discrepancy existing between the position of the superintendent or post office inspector in Prince Edward Island and that in other districts in Canada, and to ask why the classification for one district should be different from that of others.

That matter has been up for consideration by the department for some time, on the application of the inspector himself. Mr. Whear, I think, cannot expect to have the same salary classification as inspectors in the larger districts. The district of Prince Edward Island is a limited district in comparison with Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, and he has been notified that he cannot expect to have the same salary rating as the district superintendents of those two provinces. Further than that, the matter has been laid before .the Civil Service Commission, and their decision is that they will not consent to an increased salary at the present time, based on the reasons I have given.

I quite understand the reasons as given by the Postmaster General, but .there are other considerations that I should like to bring to his notice. The post office inspector in that district has probably more work to do, involving greater responsibility than have inspectors in the other districts, for the reason that he alone of the inspectors has no assistants.
I will go into it further with the commission, but that was their decision.

For a great many years that district was recognized as being on the same footing as the other districts. It is true that when the classification came into effect in 1921 the district was abolished altogether and attached to New Brunswick for a short period. However, during the fall of that same year the arrangement was found to be so very unsatisfactory to the island people that the district was reinstated, but left in a different classification. I am not particularly interested in the official at all, but I do feel that as a matter of provincial rights the province should at least be on the same footing in this regard as the other provinces. I feel that further consideration ought
to be given to this matter. We are recognized in other respects. For instance, until this year the same discrimination existed with regard to taxation, but the Island has now been established as a separate district with an inspector of taxation. I think the Post Office department in conjunction with the Civil Service Commission should find some means of establishing a similar condition in regard to our post office inspector. Our supreme court judges and others in the provincial service are on the same footing as similar officials in other parts of Canada. Is there not same means whereby this district may be dealt with similarly as a matter of provincial rights?
I will give it my attention.

I will be very brief, Mr. Chairman. I desire to bring to the attention of the minister some very important harbour and river improvements in the public service in the county of Cumberland. Last session I mentioned to the minister that at Port Greville, on the bay of Fundy, a good deal of money a few years years ago was spent in improving the breakwater. The information that has come to me-and I am sure it must be in the possession of the department-is that the breakwater does not extend far enough out to prove of sufficient advantage to the shipping interests at that point. In addition to that, during a very severe storm last fall the beach protection, which joins the breakwater at a certain point, was completely washed out, making harbour conditions at this point very hazardous. I appeal to the minister again to give immediate consideration to this matter, because Port Greville is not served by a railway. A great deal of shipping is carried on at this point, particulars of which I gave the house last year, and this port is in the centre of a lumbering district. I think the 3onditions there should be brought up to a standard which will enable people using that accommodation to carry on their regular jusinesss with efficiency.
There is another point along the shore of the bay of Fundy where improvements are also necessary in connection with a wharf;
I refer to Spencer's Island. I am not going into particulars to-night but merely mention this case in order that the minister might make a note of it and possibly include an item in the supplementary estimates to take care of this work.
Another matter to which I will direct attention is a wharf which has been requested by the citizens of Northport. This village is on the Northumberland straits, and I believe a petition was forwarded to the minister within the last few months urging that a wharf be built. This is a very important fishing district and there is no accommodation at this point of any kind. The people there feel themselves justified in requesting that some assistance be granted them by way of a wharf; it need not be an expensive affair, but 
a small wharf will enable them to carry on their regular business much more efficiently.
I also spoke to the minister in connection with the wharf at Pugwash, which is also on the Northumberland straits. That wharf is in a very dilapidated condition. As a matter of fact there are two wharves at this point, one owned by the railway company and the other by the government, and my information is that both these wharves require immediate attention. This is also an important port, and I believe petitions have been forwarded requesting that this accommodation be brought up to a certain standard.
The last matter about which I wish to speak concerns the dredging in the inner and outer harbour at Parrsboro, which is on the bay of Fundy. I believe the minister has received communications from the board of trade in this town and from other prominent citizens urging that immediate action be taken to dredge the harbour in order to enable the business of this .port to be carried on freely and to the general advantage of all concerned. I wish to impress upon the minister the importance of this port, which also needs a government wharf in the town. There is a government wharf a Short distance outside the town but it does not properly serve the shipping interests, since a great deal of lumber and other material is shipped from this centre. There are some privately owned wharves at this point but they are in a run-down condition and are not properly serving the shipping public. That is all I have to say; I appeal to the minister to give these matters his immediate attention and, if possible, to place amounts in the supplementary estimates this year to bring these works up to a proper standard and in order that the shipping interests to be served may be able to take full advantage of the accommodation offered.

May I suggest to the minister that the house adjourn now, because a number of the Nova Scotia members on this side thought we would not get through the Post Office estimates in time to deal with anything else to-night, and they particularly requested the hon. member for Argenteuil and myself to ask the minister not to take up anything else to-night. There is only ten minutes left, anyway.
